Following Donald Trump’s election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Under the new US administration, the direction of US policy may undergo two fundamental shifts — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to deglobalisation — which could have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. Notably, emerging market economies face heightened risks amid a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar and the possible adoption of trade protectionist measures by the US. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank rates rose in tandem with US dollar interbank rates. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained favourable, and overall loan growth accelerated further in the second half of 2016. The residential property market showed signs of correction immediately after the introduction of the new stamp duty measure, but has picked up recently. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the implications of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes and, more broadly, US policy uncertainty, particularly the risk of substantial fund outflows and their potential impact on local interest rates. Following Donald Trump’s election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only did the election result surprise the market, but the associated market reaction was also unexpected. In particular, expectations that the Trump administration’s tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending and deregulation would boost US economic growth drove global equity markets higher. Under the new US administration, the direction of US policy may undergo two fundamental shifts — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to deglobalisation — which could have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. However, the Trump tax cuts anticipated by the market may not provide the expected boost to US economic growth. In particular, with US economic activity already close to its potential, fiscal stimulus may provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth while exacerbating upside risks to US inflation. While it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (Fed) will therefore significantly accelerate the pace of monetary tightening, long-term bond yields have already risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. Meanwhile, rising trade protectionism would result in a “lose-lose” outcome for both the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would create market distortions that undermine overall welfare, impede global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the still-fragile recovery in Europe. For emerging market economies, the risk of fund outflows arising from a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation has increased. This could weigh on economic growth and exacerbate the risk of abrupt fund outflows. Indeed, amid expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration and concerns over surging energy prices, markets have repriced inflation risks, leading to broad-based and marked increases in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign debt markets of 26 selected economies. The findings suggest that the influence of the US Treasury market on sovereign debt markets has deepened since the 2013 “taper tantrum”, and that US interest rate hikes and tighter financial conditions would have significant impacts on both advanced economies and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016 as exports recovered, while the earlier market volatility arising from concerns over possible policy changes under the new US administration — including regional currency depreciation and rising sovereign yields — only began to stabilise in early 2017. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but faces heightened risks and uncertainties. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation and increased financial market volatility could lead to tighter financial conditions. Meanwhile, the US may adopt protectionist policies that could affect regional economies, although the actual impact remains unclear at present. In Mainland China, overall economic growth edged up in the second half of 2016 amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and improving private-sector business spending. Although the economy continued to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainty remained over the Mainland’s growth outlook. In particular, given the Government’s determination to curb housing price increases, the real estate sector may make a smaller contribution to growth this year if the property market continues to cool. Meanwhile, the continued advancement of economic restructuring and changes in China-US trade relations may increase uncertainty over the near-term economic outlook. Externally, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private-sector economic activity, some concerns remained in the market over the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given that M1 growth accelerated while M2 growth slowed. Box 2 (see page 24) examines whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) explores the factors that may have caused the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and that the significantly faster growth of M1 than M2 mainly reflected a decline in the opportunity cost of holding liquid money as a result of monetary easing in recent years, as well as a possible increase in precautionary demand for money amid heightened economic uncertainty. Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. Externally, growth in exports of goods increased alongside improving regional trade flows, while exports of services grew steadily amid a recovery in trade-related and transportation services. As imports of goods and services grew faster, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half. With economic growth picking up, the headline unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. The Government and market consensus forecast real GDP growth of 2–3% and 2.0%, respectively, for 2017. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook continues to face significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased the downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong’s external demand. Amid appreciation pressure on the US dollar and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, global financial conditions are expected to become less supportive of the real economy and could lead to tighter local financial conditions, particularly if tail risks materialise. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the construction of a financial conditions index for Hong Kong to facilitate the monitoring of local financial conditions. Local inflationary pressures have remained moderate since the second half of 2016, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum picked up slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rentals. With stable import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, although it weakened intermittently following the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. Alongside US dollar appreciation, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate rose further. Given the sizeable Monetary Base, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates remained low, but increased from October onwards due to year-end funding demand and the need to catch up with US dollar interest rate hikes. Accordingly, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage business, the average mortgage rate edged up to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% in the first half. The growth was supported by stronger local economic activity and increased year-end financing needs of multinational corporations. Domestic loan growth picked up slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a modest decline in the first half. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans increased by 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayments of foreign currency loans. Banks’ funding positions remained broadly sound. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting faster deposit growth than loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 59.9% at the end of the year, while the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio fell markedly to 63.8% on strong growth in US dollar deposits. Amid a strong US dollar, both the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool, comprising customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit, consolidated further along with other offshore renminbi markets, while CNH HIBOR volatility increased significantly. Nevertheless, banks’ renminbi liquidity management remained sound, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business will likely continue to face headwinds arising from uncertainty over the renminbi exchange rate. As global market conditions improved, the Hong Kong equity market closed markedly higher during the review period. Although the US presidential election produced an unexpected result, the market experienced only a brief shock. This was mainly because investor expectations of fiscal stimulus under the Trump administration drove global equity markets higher. While benefiting from this development, the local market remained cautiously optimistic, possibly due to concerns over a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges to the Mainland economic outlook, uncertainty over renminbi policy and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuation could provide support. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply towards the end of last year and their yield spreads over US Treasuries widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar debt market continued to expand steadily during the review period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi bond market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, although new bond issuance for the year as a whole remained lower than in the preceding year. Looking ahead, both the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets would come under pressure if global investors reverse their earlier yield-seeking investment strategies. With US trade policy still unclear and the renminbi exchange rate likely to remain volatile, the outlook for both debt markets over the next six months remains subject to significant uncertainties. The residential property market showed signs of correction immediately after the Government introduced the new stamp duty measure, but has picked up recently. In view of renewed market exuberance, the Government raised the stamp duty rate uniformly to 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets declined in the following two months. However, transaction volume has increased recently, partly reflecting an increase in new launches by developers. Meanwhile, property prices continued to reach new highs, albeit at a slower pace.

US policy uncertainty increased following Trump’s surprise election as US President. Although market attention focused on the near-term benefits of potentially large-scale fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, US economic activity was already close to its potential, and fiscal stimulus might provide only a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth while further exacerbating upside risks to inflation. More importantly, risks facing emerging market economies were increasing amid fund outflow pressures arising from a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while potential US trade protectionist measures would also threaten global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, with export volumes also increasing recently. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are likely to remain volatile, with increasing downside risks to economic growth. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016 amid robust infrastructure investment growth and improved private-sector business spending. The Mainland economy continued to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, but the ongoing economic restructuring and changes in China-US trade relations could increase uncertainty surrounding the near-term economic outlook. Given the Government’s determination to curb housing price increases, the real estate sector’s contribution to economic growth might also decline this year if the property market continues to cool. Externally, although the RMB remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) currency basket during the review period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, before apparently easing slightly in early 2017. Global financial markets reacted strongly to Trump’s surprise election as US President. In particular, market expectations that Trump’s policies, including tax reform, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending and deregulation, would boost US economic growth and inflation drove major equity markets higher (Chart 2.1). Consequently, rising market expectations of US inflation and US interest rate hikes led to a sharp increase in US Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar. Chart 2.1 Equity market indices of selected advanced economies However, the anticipated Trump tax cuts might not have as much of a positive impact on US economic growth as markets expected. Although a shift in economic policy towards reliance on fiscal easing would help relieve the heavy burden on monetary easing, whether this is the appropriate time to implement fiscal easing is debatable given the current stage of the US economic cycle. Although US economic growth slowed in recent quarters, the output gap gradually narrowed, and the unemployment rate in February was in line with the Fed’s estimate of the natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, indicating that US economic activity was close to its potential. With the US economy currently in an expansionary cycle, the fiscal multiplier would be lower than during an economic downturn (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. Indeed, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital might result in lower tax revenues (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any event, with diminishing spare capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth could drive up inflation even if their real impact on economic growth were limited. Meanwhile, other factors, such as rising oil and commodity prices and potential trade protectionist measures, including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, might also exacerbate upside risks to US inflation. Despite the increased risk of rising US inflation, the Fed remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and inclined to maintain its ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields had already risen, partly reflecting increased inflation risk in the US. Since the US election, although market projections of the future federal funds rate had been revised upwards to levels close to the Fed’s median projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remained well below the Fed’s longer-term projection (Chart 2.2). Therefore, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes could pose a risk of significant market volatility. While financial markets focused on the near-term benefits of stronger US economic growth driven by potentially expansionary fiscal policies and business-friendly measures, longer-term risks remained, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further increase in US government debt. Indeed, the Trump administration might fulfil its election pledge to adopt trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would create market distortions that reduce overall welfare, impede global trade flows, lower the efficiency of global supply chains and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future federal funds rate projections: Fed versus market In Europe, political instability remained a major risk and impediment to the European economic recovery. Although economic conditions in the Euro area improved gradually, with real GDP growing moderately by 1.7% year-on-year in the fourth quarter, only slightly below the 1.8% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, economic activity in the Euro area remained only slightly above its pre-global financial crisis level, in contrast to the stronger US economic recovery (Chart 2.3). Since the UK’s decision to leave the European Union last summer, markets had been concerned about an eventual break-up of the Euro area. Although Italy’s economic and political situation appeared to have stabilised after the formation of a new government and the implementation of measures to rescue the banking sector, the forthcoming elections in Germany and France, and possibly Italy, could become political flashpoints amid Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, European sovereign yields continued to rise and corporate bond spreads also widened, particularly in peripheral countries, potentially creating a vicious cycle for the real economy and placing pressure on real business investment in the Euro area. Chart 2.3 Real GDP of major advanced economies In Japan, following upward revisions to real GDP in recent quarters, year-on-year growth rose to 1.6% in the fourth quarter of 2016, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating that the economic recovery was stronger than previously expected. However, partly due to structural problems in the labour market, sluggish wage growth resulted in weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the recent rapid depreciation of the Japanese yen suggested that the downward pressure on “new core” goods inflation from the earlier appreciation of the yen would soon begin to dissipate. Together with the stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicated an improvement in the near-term inflation outlook, and “new core” inflation, excluding fresh food and energy, was expected to bottom out and recover after falling to 0.1% in December. Nevertheless, amid long-term and structural headwinds, growth was likely to remain slow, while inflation expectations remained at around 0.5%–0.6%, below the level prevailing when Abenomics was introduced in early 2014. The risk therefore remained that inflation would fail to reach the Bank of Japan’s medium-term target of 2%. For other countries, particularly emerging market economies, the benefits of faster US economic growth through the trade channel might be smaller because of reduced US imports following the global financial crisis and the possibility that the US might implement protectionist policies. Meanwhile, a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation would tighten financial conditions and exacerbate downside risks to economic growth. This could weigh on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, together with concerns over a sharp increase in energy prices, led to a repricing of inflation risk and broad-based, significant increases in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economic activity regained momentum recently, with a modest increase in regional GDP and rising inflation. Real GDP growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable, supported by steady private consumption in many regional economies. Meanwhile, exports generally increased modestly from their lows in 2015. This benefited not only from the stabilisation of growth in China, but also from improved performance in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters such as Malaysia and Indonesia, the rebound in commodity prices provided an additional boost. Other major exporters, such as South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, also regained momentum on the back of growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — As commodity prices, particularly oil prices, rebounded, producer price inflation generally trended upwards. Although this would raise industrial costs and possibly consumer spending, consumption and investment growth might increase as the risk of prolonged deflation diminished. Faster producer price inflation might exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which producer price increases were passed through to consumer prices, which varied across economies. Consensus forecasts for CPI inflation indicated that inflation in many regional economies, while remaining slightly below their respective central banks’ inflation targets for 2017, would rise closer to target levels (Chart 2.4). Central banks in East Asia generally maintained accommodative monetary policies with unchanged interest rates, except Bank Indonesia, which cut rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth. Chart 2.4 Headline CPI inflation, projections and central bank targets in East Asia Despite the improvement in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 triggered short-term financial market volatility. Foreign exchange markets — Following the US presidential election, most regional currencies weakened against the US dollar as investors expected higher US inflation. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies depreciated by less or even appreciated slightly following the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Spot FX depreciation against the US dollar versus changes in nominal effective exchange rates following the US election Bond and equity markets — Asset prices declined briefly following the US presidential election but stabilised shortly thereafter. Spreads between sovereign yields in East Asian economies and US Treasury yields increased. However, as markets stabilised, yields in some regional economies declined but remained above their pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, spreads narrowed from their pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads between 10-year sovereign yields and US Treasury yields Portfolio investment flows — Portfolio capital flowed out of East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the “taper tantrum” in mid-2013. Capital inflows resumed in the first few weeks of 2017, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth was expected to remain stable, albeit below its historical average. With heightened uncertainty surrounding US government policies and the Fed’s potential policy responses, financial markets were likely to remain volatile. Sharp increases in the US dollar and yields might attract capital from the region to the US, prompting investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, particularly those already carrying high valuations. The resulting tightening of financial conditions would also place debt repayment pressure on corporates with large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. At the macro level, broad-based increases in global interest rates would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, which would not only weigh on aggregate demand in the short term but might also affect potential growth over the longer term. Finally, regional exporters faced the potential threat of trade protectionist policies under the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies had continued to widen in recent years (Chart 2.7), particularly in the region’s key export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, garments and textiles. Over the past two decades, increased US imports in these industries had been accompanied by substantial job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalising US manufacturing could pose significant risks to regional exporters.

Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016, driven by faster growth in private consumption and buoyant public-sector building and construction activities. Given the increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth is expected to be moderate in 2017. Inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained, supported by stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum. Hong Kong’s economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 1.2% quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly faster than the 0.8% growth in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly reflecting improved consumer confidence and resilient labour market conditions, private consumption growth accelerated and became the main driver of GDP growth. Building and construction activities also became buoyant, supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport. However, weak corporate capital spending reduced the contribution of aggregate investment spending to GDP growth. On the external front, both exports and imports of goods grew at faster rates alongside increased regional trade flows (Chart 3.2).22 Trade-related and transportation services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly due to strong travel demand among local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions by major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% during the first three quarters before edging down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). Indeed, the unemployment rates of several major sectors declined in the second half of the year, including the retail, accommodation and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector stabilised. Total employment reached a record high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, global economic and trade growth may remain moderate amid uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial environment. Coupled with an increase in the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate due to the strong US dollar, this will constrain Hong Kong’s export performance. Domestically, while stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately as interest rates rise. Building and construction activities should grow steadily amid increased housing supply and the planned commencement of several infrastructure projects, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will restrain corporate capital spending. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% in 2017, while private-sector analysts’ projections average 2.0%. The growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those arising from the external environment. Policy uncertainty under the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, with possible trade protectionist policies posing headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect flows of Hong Kong dollar funds. In addition, US interest rate normalisation will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, local inflation has remained moderate overall despite stronger sequential momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 through January this year (Chart 3.4). The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which measures inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before edging down to 2.4% in January. The stronger inflation momentum was mainly attributable to increases in tradable goods prices and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, tradable goods price inflation rose from negative territory in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by prices of basic foodstuffs and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, the CCPI housing rental component rose from the third quarter onwards as the decline in private housing rentals narrowed and public housing rentals were raised in September 2016, before moderating slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major component Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rentals In the near term, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained amid weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures. Imported inflation should remain low, as the strength of the Hong Kong dollar will partly offset the impact of the rebound in global commodity prices (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap was estimated to have remained close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thereby contain services component inflation. Despite the tight labour market, wage growth was modest in recent quarters, with real payroll per person engaged rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before declining by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Against the backdrop of cautious business sentiment arising from persistent uncertainties in the external environment, increases in labour costs should be restrained. In addition, given the weak retail sales performance in recent months, growth in retail property rentals is expected to be moderate. Moreover, the effects of the earlier easing in private housing rentals will gradually feed through, also helping to alleviate inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is expected to decline in 2017. The Government forecasts underlying inflation of 2.0% for the year, lower than the 2.3% recorded in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour costs and real payroll per person engaged The inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation in the US accelerates under the Trump administration, US interest rates may rise faster than expected, potentially pushing up local mortgage interest rates and increasing downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. Meanwhile, appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may keep import prices weak and make Hong Kong less attractive to inbound visitors. On the upside, if the global economy expands faster than expected, Hong Kong’s economic growth may accelerate and demand-driven international commodity prices may rise, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. In addition, the increased Statutory Minimum Wage will take effect on 1 May 2017, which may further raise inflation, although the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed through to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong dollar interbank rates rose alongside US dollar interbank rates. Partly due to improvements in the local economic environment, overall loans continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalisation, uncertainty over the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November led to broad declines in Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections released by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on 13–14 December 2016 heightened market expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened alongside other Asian currencies, but began to show signs of weakening from mid-February as market expectations of a US interest rate hike in March increased. The Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered during the reporting period (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators Amid the strength of the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) rose by 4.9% between August and December before stabilising recently (Chart 4.3). As the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners had only a limited impact, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) closely tracked the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics show that non-residents’ investments in equity and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and a large number of initial public offerings (Table 4.A). However, partly driven by increased holdings of US bonds by Hong Kong banks, residents’ debt investments recorded sizeable outflows that more than offset the investment inflows from non-residents. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds indicated portfolio investment outflows in the final quarter of 2016, mainly because the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election and expectations of faster US interest rate hikes put the local financial market and other Asian markets under pressure (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data indicate that portfolio investment in Hong Kong experienced fund inflow pressure in the first quarter of 2017, partly because investors’ optimism about expansionary fiscal policy in the US supported improvements in global financial markets. Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalisation would increase the risk of a reversal in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Meanwhile, uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process and elections in EU member states may increase fund flow volatility. In addition, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert fund inflow pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading initially exceeded southbound trading following the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite higher US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable and increased further by 1.7% in the second half, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly stable at the high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Within the total, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly, as an additional HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills were issued to meet banks’ strong demand for liquidity management. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base With the local economy becoming more resilient, the growth of the Hong Kong dollar money supply accelerated. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half to 6.5% in the second half. As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand amid stronger local economic activity and a recovery in initial public offering activities. Analysed by counterparts, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks’ net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), representing respectively money created through credit expansion and net inflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterparts Meanwhile, growth in foreign currency deposits continued to vary. After increasing by 10.2% in the first half, US dollar deposits recorded a stronger increase of 12.8% in the second half amid a strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted further by 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, growth in total deposits with authorized institutions accelerated to 6.2% in the second half of 2016, while full-year growth was 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation, banks’ wholesale funding costs increased in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained low, they increased partly because of year-end funding demand and a catch-up with the rise in US dollar interbank rates. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards alongside the US dollar yield curve, with the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rising by around 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at the end of December. In early 2017, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally declined as funding demand eased, while yields on longer-term Hong Kong Government Bonds edged down alongside US Treasury yields. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar interbank rates and the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond Given the banking system’s sizeable deposit base, increases in retail interest rates were relatively small. Banks’ average funding cost, as measured by the composite interest rate, remained low, edging up by only 6 basis points from seven months earlier to 0.32% in January 2017 (Chart 4.9). Amid relatively stable funding costs and intensified competition in the mortgage business, the average lending rate for new mortgages fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016 before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 alongside the rise in HIBOR. Chart 4.9 Composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Looking ahead, the pace of increase in local interest rates will depend on the speed of US interest rate normalisation, the scale of fund outflows and global macro-financial developments. Upward pressure on local interest rates, together with the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar REER alongside the US dollar exchange rate, may reduce the support provided by local financial conditions to the real economy. Box 4 discusses the construction of a Hong Kong financial conditions index for monitoring local financial conditions. Amid stronger local economic activity and increased cross-border financing demand, total loans increased further by 4.2% in the second half after growing by 2.2% in the first half (Chart 4.10). With economic growth gaining momentum, domestic loan growth accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half after edging down in the first half, partly reflecting increased year-end funding demand from multinational corporations. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans also recorded moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayments of foreign currency loans. Total loans grew moderately by 6.5% in 2016 as a whole, compared with 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Analysed by economic sector, domestic loans showed mixed performance in the second half (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial and finance-related corporations and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half, reflecting to some extent strong financing demand driven by the more favourable growth outlook for these sectors. Loans for building, construction and property development also grew at a faster pace alongside increased private-sector construction activity. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade financing and loans to the manufacturing, wholesale and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans by selected sector Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half from 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, rose by 7.2%, partly reflecting improvements in the economic environment (Chart 4.11), while growth in residential mortgage loans accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting buoyant residential transactions between July and October. As a result, the household debt-to-GDP ratio also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Household debt-to-GDP ratio and its components Banks’ funding conditions remained broadly stable. Reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged down from 78.2% at the end of June 2016 to 77.1% at the end of the year (Chart 4.13). Meanwhile, the overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined from 61.4% to 59.9% at the end of the year, with the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio falling markedly to 63.8% amid strong growth in US dollar deposits. Chart 4.13 Loan-to-deposit ratios Credit growth will remain uncertain in the period ahead amid expectations of higher interest rates and rapid changes in the macro-financial environment. The HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook indicates that loan demand will remain soft in the near term. Both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened amid US dollar appreciation (Chart 4.14). The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of late 2016, closing at a year-low of 6.98 against the US dollar at the end of 2016. The CNH interbank market again experienced liquidity tightness in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks’ precautionary funding demand ahead of the year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid deteriorating market sentiment, the overnight CNH HIBOR once surged to 61.3% on 6 January 2017. The increase in CNH funding costs subsequently led to the unwinding of short CNH positions, driving a rally in the CNH exchange rate in early January 2017 and causing the CNH-CNY spread to shift to a premium. Since mid-January, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates have stabilised somewhat, while liquidity conditions have gradually improved, with the overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR declining to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively at the end of February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared with the same period in 2015, due to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a decrease in loan impairment charges. Banks’ capital positions and asset quality also remained sound. Although HIBORs rose notably following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Retail banks’ funding costs remained stable and low on the back of a large retail deposit base. Nevertheless, banks should carefully assess the impact of a potentially faster-than-expected US rate hike path, particularly the risk of substantial capital outflows and their subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. In addition, given the continued rise in the leverage of non-local corporates, a sharp increase in interest rates could lead to deterioration in banks’ asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against system-wide risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio requirement will be increased to 1.875% with effect from 1 January 2018. The profitability of retail banks improved, with the return on assets rising to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 (red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profit was attributable to growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a decrease in loan impairment charges. For 2016 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose to 1.10% from 1.05% in 2015. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks continued to improve, reaching 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Hong Kong’s wholesale funding costs rose notably following the resumption of US interest rate hikes in December 2016. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR increased notably by 33 basis points in December 2016, although it remained low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates Nevertheless, the overall impact of the US interest rate hike on retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs remained modest. This was because retail deposits were the primary source of funding for retail banks, and retail deposit rates remained stable and low even after the interest rate hike. Against this backdrop, after remaining at a low level of around 0.26% for more than a year, the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, edged up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong exhibited a similar picture. Although banks’ average non-deposit market funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, their average deposit funding costs in the retail market increased by a smaller 11 basis points. Overall, the average aggregate Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks increased by 17 basis points (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The magnitude and speed of the increase in HIBORs exceeded those of Hong Kong banks’ funding costs, which could benefit some retail banks. This was because they had actively promoted HIBOR-based mortgages over the past few years, and the increase in interest rates on such loans could help widen their overall net interest margins. However, the improvement in net interest margins could be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. Indeed, there were signs that some banks had reduced their mortgage spreads over the benchmark and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. In the longer term, with further US interest rate hikes, banks may soon face upward pressure on retail deposit rates, thereby affecting their funding costs and having a more notable impact on net interest margins. Banks’ capitalisation remained strong and well above international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a high level of 19.2% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital adequacy ratio was 16.4%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. The revised capital adequacy framework under Basel III, which locally incorporated AIs are required to comply with, took effect on 1 January 2013. Therefore, the capital adequacy ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with the data up to December 2012. The liquidity position of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, remained sound during the reporting period. Although the average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions edged down from 158.0% in the second quarter of 2016 to 156.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016, it remained at a high level (Chart 5.6). The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios remained well above their respective minimum regulatory requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector was able to withstand liquidity shocks arising from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for retail banks. The share of customer deposits in banks’ total liabilities increased from 71.7% at the end of June 2016 to 73.1% at the end of December 2016 (Chart 5.7). Chart 5.7 Liability structure of retail banks As retail banks’ total loans and advances and total deposits grew at similar rates during the reporting period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio remained stable at 57.0% in December 2016 (Chart 5.8). Over the same period, the Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratios also remained broadly unchanged. Chart 5.8 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of retail banks Although the interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks increased slightly, it remained at a low level. Estimates suggest that, under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions could decline by an amount equivalent to 3.92% of their total capital base in December 2016 (Chart 5.9). Nevertheless, given that the pace of US interest rate normalisation could be faster than expected following the US presidential election, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. The interest rate shock refers to a standard 200-basis-point parallel interest rate shock to an institution’s interest rate risk exposure. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of banks’ total capital base. During the reporting period, the asset quality of retail banks’ loan portfolios remained sound, with the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans staying low at 0.72% and 0.53% respectively at the end of December 2016. Both ratios remained low by historical standards (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10 Asset quality of retail banks Although current asset quality remained sound by historical standards, banks in Hong Kong should continue to monitor the external environment. As the assessment in Box 5 shows, the rapid growth in banking-sector loans for use outside Hong Kong since the global financial crisis suggests that banks’ asset quality has become more susceptible to the external environment. Banks had mixed expectations about credit growth in the near term. The HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2016 showed that, although most surveyed AIs expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, the share of surveyed AIs expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months edged up to 14% (Table 5.A). In the second half of 2016, the credit risk associated with unsecured household exposure remained contained, with the year-to-date annualised credit card charge-off ratio and the delinquency ratio declining to 1.92% and 0.24% respectively at the end of December (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio for credit card lending and bankruptcy petitions Banks’ mortgage portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at 0.03% at the end of December. The average LTV ratio of newly approved mortgages was 51.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio was well below the 64% recorded in September 2009, before the HKMA began implementing seven rounds of countercyclical macroprudential measures. However, the debt-servicing index47 for new mortgages increased from 44.0 in the second quarter of 2016 to 48.8 in the fourth quarter (red line in Chart 5.12), mainly reflecting an increase in the average size of new mortgages (Chart 5.13). Continued US interest rate normalisation could further increase household debt burdens. A sensitivity test showed that, if interest rates rose by 300 basis points with other conditions unchanged, the index could increase significantly to 67.3 within four quarters.48 Banks should remain vigilant against the risk of a continued increase in household debt burdens. Chart 5.12 Average LTV ratio of new mortgages and household debt burden Chart 5.13 New mortgages of surveyed AIs The US rate hike path remained a key factor affecting the credit risk of corporate exposures. However, the actual impact on an individual bank’s asset quality would depend on the characteristics of its corporate loan portfolio. In particular, our assessment based on the accounting data of Hong Kong-listed non-financial corporates found that the leverage ratios of local and non-local corporates had diverged markedly since the global financial crisis, with non-local corporates more susceptible to debt-servicing difficulties.50 Banks should assess the impact of interest rate hikes on the credit risk of their exposures to non-local corporates. Specifically, corporate leverage, as measured by the weighted average debt-to-equity ratio, increased after the global financial crisis, driven mainly by non-local corporates. The leverage ratio of non-local corporates rose to 85% in the first half of 2016 (red line in Chart 5.14), while that of local corporates remained broadly stable. As markets reassessed US inflation risks, volatility returned to global financial markets at the beginning of the year. In February, global equity markets plunged from their end-January peaks, fully reversing the notable gains made at the beginning of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The sustained rally in global equity markets amid low volatility over the past two years was underpinned by market expectations of an ideal environment featuring continued steady economic growth and low inflation and interest rates. However, these expectations are being challenged by the risks of tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while markets continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total lending continued to increase in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace. Following a modest slowdown in the middle of last year, both housing price growth and transaction volumes picked up in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, renewed volatility in global and local financial markets may add to fluctuations in Hong Kong’s fund flows. Given uncertainties in financial markets, the normalisation of US monetary policy and lingering geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant to the risks of greater interest rate volatility and potential fund outflows. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality of larger-than-expected interest rate increases. After the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) had hovered at low levels for more than two years, volatility returned to global financial markets at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their end-January peaks, with the S&P 500 Index at one point dropping by more than 10%, fully reversing the notable gains recorded in early January. The shift in market sentiment was attributable to signs that the global economic recovery might exert pressure on persistently subdued US wages and prices, potentially prompting the Fed to accelerate its rate hike path. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rally in global equity markets over the past two years was founded on market expectations that favourable economic conditions would persist. Global economic growth momentum continued to strengthen in the second half of 2017, with a synchronised pickup in economic activity across advanced and emerging market economies. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package that included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and individual tax rules, fuelling market expectations that the robust US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite stronger activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would remain low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rallied notably in 2017, with the US equity market in particular repeatedly reaching record highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-lived financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In the US, the economy has now reached its potential output, and the expected cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts may accelerate the rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Fed to tighten monetary policy more rapidly. At the same time, as the tax cuts will increase the budget deficit, the US may issue more Treasury securities in the future, which is expected to exert greater upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Fed continues to normalise its balance sheet. Outside the US, strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect their central banks to scale back their quantitative easing programmes. If materialised, this would lead to a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also cloud the global growth outlook. The US Government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including announcements of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns about whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Moreover, an unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could affect global trade and increase global financial market volatility. Given the above uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlook, the sustainability of the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets is in question. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical increase in global demand and the anticipated rise in the US budget deficit resulting from tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); together with an expected increase in the term premium arising from the Fed’s balance sheet normalisation, this may raise long-term interest rates and weigh on asset market valuations. In East Asia, regional economies also enjoyed an ideal environment of robust growth and moderate inflation. Alongside favourable economic performance and an optimistic outlook, capital inflows accelerated and financial markets rallied. However, this favourable outlook is subject to downside risks arising from tightening global liquidity as major central banks proceed with monetary policy normalisation in tandem; the US Government’s inward-looking trade policies; geopolitical tensions; and potentially tighter offshore US dollar liquidity as US corporates repatriate profits on a large scale in response to the one-off “deemed repatriation” provision under the US tax reform. Any shock to credit and financial markets could trigger a reversal of fund flows, with highly leveraged sectors and economies being most vulnerable to tightening financial conditions. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by robust consumption, strong infrastructure spending and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year. Meanwhile, signs of the rise of the “new economy” became increasingly evident, with sectors such as high-value-added manufacturing and services showing strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the “new economy” can help offset the near-term pressure on growth arising from further structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced that they would maintain a proactive fiscal policy stance in 2018, which may help cushion adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and the containment of system-wide risks. In particular, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, especially in first-tier cities. Meanwhile, banks’ exposures to corporates in overcapacity sectors remained contained as banks tightened lending standards, while shadow banking activity also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to these positive developments, our analysis also suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints facing state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capability appear to have tightened, possibly because of reduced support from local governments (see Box 2 on page 28 for details). On the external front, fund outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017 amid stabilising economic conditions and reduced risks. The Hong Kong economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for 2017 as a whole, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Private consumption remained robust in the second half of 2017, supported by favourable employment and income conditions and rising asset prices. Aggregate investment spending also rebounded on increased corporate capital spending. On the external front, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018, with private consumption, building and construction activity, and exports continuing to support growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. The Government and market consensus forecast real GDP growth of 3%–4% and 3.0% respectively for 2018. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, Mainland China’s economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, and movements in local asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to a nearly 20-year low of 2.9%, local inflationary pressures remained contained. Nevertheless, sequential inflation momentum has shown signs of edging up in recent months, with increases in the prices of both tradable goods and services. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up to a still-moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through of rising fresh-letting private residential rentals. Funding demand arising from initial public offering activities and seasonal factors tightened liquidity conditions, while increased unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions caused the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity conditions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities resumed, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again from December 2017. In early 2018, the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable despite volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. HIBORs faced upward pressure between September and December 2017, mainly because of funding demand from initial public offering activities and banks’ prudent approach to liquidity management towards the year-end. In December, the average overnight and three-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively from six months earlier to 0.25% and 1.26%. After edging down in early January 2018, HIBORs remained broadly stable and were unaffected by the recent correction in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage market, banks’ average lending rate for new mortgages followed the rise in short-term HIBORs and increased to 2.16% in December. Meanwhile, retail banks’ funding costs generally remained low after a temporary increase in October due to initial public offering activities, with the composite interest rate standing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure as US monetary policy normalisation continues, while fund flow volatility may increase in the event of an abrupt shift in global financial market sentiment. Total bank lending grew steadily by 16.1% in 2017. Following robust growth of 10.2% in the first half, loan growth moderated to 5.3% in the second half. In particular, growth in domestic loans to most sectors and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed. The moderation in foreign currency loan growth was partly attributable to higher US dollar funding costs. By contrast, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly amid favourable domestic economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs. As Hong Kong dollar loans grew faster than deposits, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose in the second half of 2017 to 82.7% at year-end, the highest level since March 2015. Meanwhile, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 63.1% at year-end amid relatively slow foreign currency loan growth. The onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilisation between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened notably against most major currencies, both the onshore and offshore renminbi strengthened against the US dollar from December onwards. Following a modest decline in the first half, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool, comprising total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit, edged up in the second half, broadly reflecting changes in market expectations of the renminbi exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi business, while renminbi loans continued to decline, the amount of renminbi trade settlement handled by banks in Hong Kong rebounded in the second half. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road initiative and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The synchronised strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 showed no signs of abating. The improved growth outlook drove global equity markets steadily higher in 2017 and early 2018. However, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, global equity markets experienced a sell-off and substantial volatility in February, marking the end of the calm conditions in financial markets over the preceding two years. Looking ahead, the risk of tighter global financial conditions and a range of policy and event risks will continue to cloud the global outlook. Amid a tight labour market, US tax cuts may accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Fed to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. As the Fed continues to normalise its balance sheet, increased issuance of US Treasury securities to finance the tax cuts may add upward pressure on long-term bond yields. The spectre of rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, supported by strong export performance and stable domestic demand, real economic growth continued to pick up in the second half of 2017. However, despite the optimistic economic outlook, it is also subject to various downside risks, such as a potentially larger-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, inward-looking US trade policies and geopolitical tensions. The materialisation of these downside risks would also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face multiple challenges, as they must guard against risks to economic growth while limiting the impact of prolonged accommodative financial conditions on inflation and balance-sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and containing system-wide risks. The near-term growth outlook remained positive but was subject to uncertainties, partly depending on the extent to which the rapid growth of the “new economy” could offset the near-term pressure on growth arising from further structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilised and risks receded, capital outflow pressure remained moderate for most of 2017. As the cyclical economic upswing became increasingly entrenched from late 2016, growth in advanced economies and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, investment and exports in the US grew solidly, supported by improved private-sector optimism and a significant weakening of the US dollar, while the Euro area and Japan also experienced broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from stabilising global commodity prices and stronger import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to receive a further boost from reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. In view of the current cyclical upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund projected in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth projections As growth momentum strengthened in the Euro area and Japan, market expectations that global monetary policy divergence would narrow, together with a more optimistic global growth outlook, boosted risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby weighing on the US dollar. Despite three rate hikes by the Fed during the year and the start of its balance-sheet normalisation, the US Dollar Index still declined by nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite the broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained weak and below their central banks’ targets, leading markets until recently to expect global interest rates to remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global equity markets continued to rise in 2017 and early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index repeatedly reaching record highs and pushing the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, its highest level since the “dot-com bubble” in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would lead to higher budget deficits and inflation had driven long-term US Treasury bond yields steadily higher, calling into question the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. A stronger-than-expected increase in average hourly earnings in the US in January 2018 prompted markets to reassess US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 Index at one point fell by more than 10% from its 26 January peak, fully reversing its significant gains at the start of the year, and remained under pressure after the US Government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index at one point jumping to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the low-volatility environment of the preceding two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, after the near-term equity market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to long-term US bond yields and possible monetary tightening by other major central banks could all lead to tighter global monetary conditions, thereby clouding the global economic outlook. First, regarding US inflation risks, the recently enacted tax reform includes several provisions that are expected to provide a short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The key measures under the tax reform include: (1) reductions in corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) a temporary allowance for the full expensing of capital investment; and (3) a one-off “deemed repatriation” provision that helps reduce incentives for US corporates to retain their overseas profits abroad. While it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now operating at its potential output, the tax cuts could push US output beyond potential, thereby leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. A larger-than-expected increase in inflationary pressure could prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. At present, the federal funds rate path expected by financial markets is shallower than the Fed’s projections. However, if inflation unexpectedly rebounds, the risk of an abrupt repricing of rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal funds rate projections Second, given that the tax reform may widen the budget deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase in the future. As the Fed continues to implement its balance-sheet normalisation plan, term premia are expected to rise; under these circumstances, increased US Treasury issuance may intensify upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Moreover, as market expectations of the passage of US tax cuts increased, US inflation expectations have risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). As a result, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased Treasury supply pressure and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 Five-year, five-year forward inflation expectations In addition, a key issue is whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low for a prolonged period as widely expected. Although estimates of R* vary, it is generally believed to have declined significantly since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, US R* may face upside risks in the future due to (1) a decline in the national saving rate resulting from the expected increase in the budget deficit; and (2) a potential rise in the investment rate arising from corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment of capital expenditure. An increase in R*, together with the expected rise in term premia resulting from the Fed’s balance-sheet normalisation, could presage higher long-term interest rates and thereby weigh on asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 US R* estimated using the Laubach-Williams model Third, stronger growth momentum in the Euro area and Japan has led markets to expect their central banks to scale back monetary easing. Should this occur, it could presage synchronised tightening in global monetary conditions. In the Euro area, member economies experienced broad-based cyclical expansions (Chart 2.7). In Japan, the economic recovery also accelerated, with real GDP recording positive growth for an eighth consecutive quarter in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continued to signal that they would maintain accommodative monetary policies amid subdued inflation, brighter growth prospects in the Euro area and Japan, together with the continued tightening of Japan’s labour market, have led some market participants to predict further tapering of their quantitative easing programmes in the near future.
