Chart 2.7 Real GDP in selected Euro area member states Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent recovery in global economic growth and trade. The US Government appears increasingly inclined to adopt inward-looking trade policies to protect domestic industries, with recent examples including the announcement in January 2018 of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines, and the announcement in early March of import tariffs on steel and aluminium, raising concerns about possible retaliatory measures by its trading partners. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom and other European Union countries are currently negotiating post-Brexit trade arrangements, a process subject to considerable uncertainty. If these developments lead to increased trade tensions, they could impede global trade flows and reduce global production efficiency. In addition, any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions, such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political instability in the Middle East and latent risks of terrorist attacks, could increase global financial market volatility. In East Asia, economic growth momentum strengthened further in the second half of 2017, ending the year on a strong note. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the main growth driver, while domestic demand also provided steady support (Chart 2.8). The accelerating recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China and a rebound in global demand for technology products all supported the region’s exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic demand and exports Inflationary pressure has remained weak thus far. In the second half of 2017, headline inflation in East Asia moderated amid lower food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, core consumer price inflation, excluding food and energy, remained low because of sluggish wage growth in several economies. Chart 2.9 East Asia: Headline and core consumer price inflation* Note: Since 2016, South Korea has set its inflation target at 2%, with a tolerance band of +/-0.5%. Sources: CEIC and respective central banks. The economic upturn, accompanied by substantial capital inflows, led to significant increases in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10). Capital inflows into regional markets rebounded markedly in 2017, with gross portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose along with the markets. Indeed, credit risk compensation in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices rose across the region. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

With buoyant domestic demand and improving export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained robust growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. The outlook for the Hong Kong economy remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including monetary policy normalisation by major central banks, global financial market stability, rising protectionist sentiment and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, while local inflationary pressures should remain moderate, some upside risks persist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter on quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, broadly similar to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow robustly and remained one of the major drivers of GDP growth. Consumption growth was robust, underpinned by favourable employment and income conditions, still-optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive wealth effect arising from rising asset prices. Despite weaker building and construction activities, increased corporate capital spending led to a notable rise in aggregate investment spending in the final quarter after remaining broadly stable for three quarters. Externally, Hong Kong’s export performance improved further, benefiting from stronger global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Chart 3.2 Exports and imports in real terms Sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment rose by around 0.7% to over 3.85 million, with the most notable increases seen in the construction sector; the financing and business services sector; and the public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. Externally, Hong Kong’s export performance will continue to benefit from an improving global growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly because of favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of a higher mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. As regards domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activities should grow steadily, supported by increased housing supply and the continued implementation of infrastructure projects. While the improving economic environment will stimulate corporate capital spending, possible interest rate increases may have an adverse impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3%–4% in 2018, while the growth estimates of international organisations and private-sector analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong’s growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in previous chapters, the performance of the Mainland economy amid tightening financial conditions, and developments in Hong Kong’s asset markets. Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, although sequential inflation momentum showed signs of a slight pickup in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index increased by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, broadly similar to the average increase of around 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The recovery in fresh-letting private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have added to inflation momentum to some extent (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures continued to remain moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per capita payroll As global inflation remains moderate and domestic cost increases are stable, Hong Kong’s inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2018, although underlying inflation may gradually pick up from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For example, inflationary pressures may increase in the second half of 2018 owing to the pass-through effect of growth in fresh-letting private residential rentals. The market consensus forecasts a moderate headline inflation rate of 2.2% for 2018, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation of 2.5%. Despite the moderate inflation outlook, upside risks remain. Externally, a larger-than-expected rise in global inflation or commodity prices could add to local inflation momentum. Domestically, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, the first time it had dropped below 3% in nearly two decades (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and any significant further tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Low interest rates following the 2008 global financial crisis led to an increase in Hong Kong households’ mortgage debt. As US dollar interest rate normalisation progresses, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually follow US dollar interest rates upwards, correspondingly increasing households’ mortgage repayment burden and thereby weighing on household consumption. This box therefore examines the impact of an increased mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt-servicing payments (i.e. interest payments plus loan principal amortisation) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of an interest rate shock to private consumption. In addition to the substitution and income effects commonly identified in economic theory, as well as the wealth and collateral effects arising from changes in asset prices, where there is a mortgage repayment burden, an interest rate shock will also affect private consumption by changing mortgage interest payments and hence households’ disposable income. This effect will increase with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans. In addition, loan principal amortisation will vary with the amount of outstanding mortgage loans, thereby also affecting private consumption through changes in households’ disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimate an outstanding mortgage debt-servicing ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the existing measure of the mortgage repayment burden, which applies only to new mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of the household sector, which is more closely related to aggregate private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the aggregate income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are respectively the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the household sector as a whole, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used measures of the repayment burden. Chart B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, together with the median ratios of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial Population Census. Both ratios trended downwards in the early 2000s, consistent with the decline in aggregate household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the housing market bubble in 1997 and the substantial fall in mortgage interest rates over the same period. Despite a sharp rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable because the HKMA’s macro-prudential measures on banks’ mortgage lending contained aggregate household mortgage leverage. In addition, the lengthening of tenors for new mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income We also compare the OMDSR with banks’ debt-servicing ratio, which is the actual debt-servicing-to-income ratio of applicants for new mortgages at banks. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks’ debt-servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. As housing prices were lower when existing mortgages were originated, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, a measure of the outstanding mortgage repayment burden covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e. the OMDSR) will be lower than a measure of the repayment burden of new mortgages (i.e. banks’ debt-servicing ratio). In addition, banks’ debt-servicing ratio is higher because, in compliance with the HKMA’s prudential supervisory requirements, banks take non-mortgage loan repayments into account when calculating the debt-servicing ratio. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks’ debt-servicing ratio remained stable, mainly because the HKMA’s prudential supervision of mortgage lending imposed a cap on banks’ debt-servicing ratio, which also helped stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks’ debt-servicing ratio for new mortgages Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used measures of the repayment burden, but is more timely and captures the burden of aggregate outstanding mortgage debt rather than only that of new mortgage debt. We therefore believe that the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the approaches of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In the model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by average real private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term in the short-run equation. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we use real income (proxied by median household income and deflated by the composite consumer price index), real housing and financial wealth (proxied respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index and deflated by the composite consumer price index), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total lending continued to increase in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Fund flow volatility may also increase if global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate traded between 7.799 and 7.827 against the US dollar (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened temporarily and stayed around 7.80 between September and November 2017. This was mainly attributable to increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ prudent liquidity management ahead of month-ends and the year-end, which tightened liquidity conditions, thereby slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. As tight Hong Kong dollar liquidity conditions eased and year-end commercial demand for US dollars increased, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Moving into 2018, the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, but the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators The Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly in line with the movements of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had only a limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index (REER), the Hong Kong dollar REER continued to closely track the movements of the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance-of-payments statistics showed that equity portfolio investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting the improved economic outlook for the region and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Debt securities investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows in debt investment by residents. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017 amid market optimism about the economic outlook and corporate earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that equity investment continued to record inflows despite the correction in global financial markets, while bond investment recorded mild fund outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalisation continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, potentially leading to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Meanwhile, given the uncertainty over the pace of US monetary policy normalisation and the rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board arrangements. Despite the Fed’s interest rate hikes and continued balance-sheet reduction, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and more recently. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued to back banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the combined total of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged at around HK$1,226.8 billion in the second half. Within the total, the Aggregate Balance decreased, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was attributable to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills, totalling HK$80 billion, to meet strong demand from banks for liquidity management. Moving into 2018, the Monetary Base remained stable despite the equity market correction. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar money supply increased further in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace. Growth in the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Demand deposits grew more rapidly during the period, partly due to buoyant asset markets and increased investment demand. An analysis of the asset counterparts showed that growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was supported by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), but was partly offset by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks’ net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in its asset counterparts Growth in foreign currency deposits, on the other hand, was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, growth in US dollar deposits slowed from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). By contrast, after declining continuously for more than two years, other foreign currency deposits rebounded markedly by 8.4% in the second half. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in renminbi deposits. As growth in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits slowed, total deposits with authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Between September and December 2017, increased funding demand from initial public offerings and banks’ prudent liquidity management ahead of month-ends and the year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and three-month HIBOR rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching monthly averages of 0.25% and 1.26% in December. The negative interest rate differentials between one- to three-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards but flattened, broadly tracking the movements of the US dollar yield curve. During the second half, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond increased by a smaller 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Moving into 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Hong Kong dollar interbank rates declined in early January as year-end funding demand subsided. Thereafter, despite corrections in global and local equity markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained broadly stable. The overnight and three-month HIBOR closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. On the retail front, although banks’ lending rates increased alongside the rise in HIBOR, their funding costs generally remained low given the still-large deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage market, banks’ average lending rate for new mortgages gradually increased by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the rise in the one-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, although the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ Hong Kong dollar funding costs, rose temporarily in October amid increased funding demand from initial public offerings, it remained soft for most of the second half and closed at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise and other major economies may also begin interest rate normalisation, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase fund flow volatility. Nevertheless, the sizeable Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base can serve as a buffer to help moderate an excessively rapid rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. In addition, banks’ prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window can also help contain excessive volatility in interbank rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. Loan growth was as high as 10.2% in the first half before slowing to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). Growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed in the second half of 2017. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half amid favourable domestic economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, while foreign currency loans edged up by only 0.1%. Within the latter, growth in US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to higher US dollar funding costs. For 2017 as a whole, total lending recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong, including trade financing, slowed from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Growth in loans for building and construction, and property development and investment, slowed in the second half, partly because the authorities required banks to strengthen risk management for lending to property developers from June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade financing and transport recorded only relatively modest growth, while loans to the wholesale and retail sector declined. By contrast, loan growth for financial and finance-related corporates remained strong, partly reflecting the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Growth in domestic loans by selected sector Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes, accelerated further to 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management customers secured by financial assets. Growth in these loans was broadly in line with the continued increase in client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with these collateralised loans were manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks on risk management for personal loans in January 2014, requiring them to adopt prudent risk management measures, including caps on loan tenor and borrowers’ debt servicing ratios. Meanwhile, despite an increase in residential transaction volume, the LTV ratio of newly approved mortgages declined, and growth in residential mortgage loans edged down to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio increased from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Retail banks’ profitability improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016, mainly due to higher net interest income. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. Credit growth moderated in the second half of 2017 following strong growth in the first half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a notable rise in HIBORs, the Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks remained low amid low retail deposit rates. However, banks should remain vigilant against the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows amid the normalisation of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued increase in corporate leverage and the high level of household indebtedness, banks should assess the potential impact of a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates on asset quality. To enhance the resilience of the banking sector against system-wide risks, Hong Kong’s countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio will be raised to 2.5% with effect from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 13.6% compared with the same period a year earlier. This was mainly due to a significant increase in net interest income and a decrease in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as assets grew faster than profit, retail banks’ return on assets edged down to 1.15% in the second half of 2017 from 1.17% in the first half. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period in 2016 (Chart 5.1). For 2017 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose to 1.16% from 1.09% in 2016. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period in 2016 (Chart 5.2). Observational evidence suggests that the improvement in the net interest margin was consistent with the increase in the average interest rate differential on Hong Kong dollar corporate loans in Hong Kong’s syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average interest rate differential on Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans Since September 2017, HIBORs have risen across the board, mainly driven by liquidity demand related to initial public offerings and from banks towards year-end, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. In particular, the three-month HIBOR reached a post-financial-crisis high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017, up by 53 basis points from the end of June, but remained low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Moving into 2018, HIBORs appeared to stabilise as banks’ year-end liquidity demand eased. Despite the recent rise in HIBORs, the Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks remained stable. This was mainly due to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, stayed low at around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up recently to 0.38% at the end of December (green line in Chart 5.4). The overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong exhibited a similar pattern. In the second half of 2017, banks’ average non-deposit market funding cost in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars rose by 35 basis points, while their average deposit funding cost increased slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks The increase in HIBORs exceeded the rise in the overall funding cost of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the interest rate differential on banks’ HIBOR-based assets. However, this improvement may be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have narrowed the spread between their mortgage rates and benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given the expectation of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. Given the intense competition in the lending market, banks’ net interest margins could come under pressure if the higher funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained well above the international minimum standard, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector remained well capitalised. At the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at the end of June (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Chart 5.6 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs The HKMA recently published a consultation paper on proposed rules prescribing loss-absorbing capacity requirements for AIs under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of AIs would benefit society by reducing the likelihood of financial crises, it would also inevitably entail costs. Box 5 provides a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of the loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment suggests that implementing the loss-absorbing capacity requirements would bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy. The liquidity position of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement, remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions rose to 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 144.2% in the second quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions edged down to 49.4% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 49.7% in the second quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of AIs suggests that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks arising from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks’ medium- and long-term funding risks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable sources of funding for their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain an NSFR of not less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for AIs, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of the total liabilities of all AIs, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all AIs The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs rose to 82.7% at the end of December 2017 from 77.1% at the end of June (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in Hong Kong dollar loans and advances than in deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 63.1% at the end of December 2017 from 65.5% at the end of June. Overall, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio rose to 73.0% from 71.4% six months earlier. Banks should assess the implications of the higher loan-to-deposit ratio for their liquidity management. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at the end of December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given the expectation that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates and proceed with balance-sheet normalisation, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of an interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks Amid a moderate but still favourable economic environment in the second half of 2017, growth in the total loans and advances of all AIs moderated to 5.3% from the strong growth of 10.2% recorded in the first half. Following two years of moderating growth, total lending grew robustly by 16.1% in 2017 as a whole. The asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At the end of December 2017, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs declined to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% at the end of June. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth of loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks’ asset quality may be more sensitive to the external environment, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks Strong credit growth is expected to continue as banks have become more optimistic about near-term credit growth. The HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2017 showed that 29% of the surveyed AIs expected loan demand to increase in the following three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). The credit risk of loans to households remained low during the review period. Banks’ mortgage portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying low at 0.03% at the end of December 2017. The average LTV ratio of newly approved mortgage loans declined further to 48.8% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 50.1% in the second quarter (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio was well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA introduced the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures in September 2009.

The global economy continued to expand, but growth momentum weakened amid heightened uncertainties arising from persistent trade tensions, tighter financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be “data dependent” and that it would be “patient”, leading investors to rule out the possibility of further interest rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, especially data that may prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. In Hong Kong, despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking by the Hong Kong dollar in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total lending growth moderated slightly in the second half of 2018, reflecting weaker credit demand amid headwinds from the ongoing China-US trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volumes falling markedly and housing prices declining, before showing signs of stabilisation in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds arising from heightened uncertainties in the external environment. Should these uncertainties intensify and persist for a prolonged period, they could significantly dampen business sentiment and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on banks’ profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact of a potential deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate exposures. The global economy continued to expand in the second half of 2018. However, while the US economy grew solidly, growth momentum weakened elsewhere. Among advanced economies, growth slowed in Japan and several major Euro area countries, while inflation remained low. Slowing global trade and a marked decline in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of weakening global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund lowered its global growth projections for 2019 and 2020 in January by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively from its October 2018 projections. Amid a dimmer growth outlook and escalating trade tensions, global equity markets experienced substantial volatility towards the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to a level unseen since the global financial crisis, raising market concerns over an imminent US recession. However, US economic fundamentals remained sound, and the likelihood of a recession in the near term was low. Nevertheless, the global economic outlook remained highly uncertain. In the US, while moderate inflation gave the Fed room to pause its interest rate hikes, the Fed’s data-dependent policy stance also implied that financial markets could become more sensitive to incoming data, especially data that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of the US-China and US-EU trade negotiations remained uncertain. In the UK, it remained uncertain whether a solution could be found to avert a “hard Brexit”. In East Asia, financial markets stabilised as the US dollar’s appreciation moderated and markets expected the Fed to pause its interest rate hikes, but a worsening external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. Indeed, weakening global trade growth had already weighed on economic growth in several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures had also eased. Although this shift could alleviate the policy dilemma facing regional central banks between supporting growth and containing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private-sector debt in some regional economies remained significant. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge facing East Asia was that an unexpected shift in the Fed’s monetary policy could generate spillovers to the sovereign debt markets of emerging market economies, including those in East Asia. In Mainland China, growth moderated further in the second half of 2018 amid heightened uncertainties in the external environment and a slight slowdown in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remained uncertain as the China-US trade negotiations had yet to reach a conclusion. A marked contraction in shadow financing activities had increased financing difficulties for private enterprises, particularly small firms, over the past few quarters, while weakening economic sentiment could also weigh on business activities. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers needed to continue balancing economic stabilisation against the containment of potential system-wide risks by adopting accommodative but targeted measures, such as targeted reserve requirement ratio cuts. Meanwhile, the authorities also introduced more supply-side measures to boost productivity growth, such as promoting competition among firms under different forms of ownership, and to provide individuals with a better social safety net. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0%–6.5%. Risk aversion dominated Mainland financial markets in 2018. Banks’ asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while leverage among listed non-financial corporates edged up. However, banks’ loan impairment charges increased further in the second half of 2018, while their exposures to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline, both of which helped shield the banking system from a potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that leverage among listed corporates in overcapacity industries—one of the major sources of bank credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors driving the recent improvement in the business performance of overcapacity industries. Compared with the first half of 2018, economic activities in Hong Kong softened in the second half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stagnated and year-on-year growth also slowed, reducing full-year economic growth from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening in economic activities mainly reflected the drag on consumption and exports from the direct or indirect effects of the China-US trade conflict. Slower private consumption growth may have reflected heightened economic uncertainties and the negative wealth effect arising from the correction in local asset prices. Externally, Hong Kong’s merchandise export performance also deteriorated, particularly after China and the US imposed additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines more closely the impact of the China-US trade conflict on Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance and discusses the near-term outlook and associated risks. Economic growth was expected to slow further in 2019, mainly due to moderating global economic growth. Amid the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong’s export performance was expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, private consumption was expected to continue supporting economic growth amid a low unemployment rate and rising household income, but the outlook for aggregate investment spending could become more uncertain. The Government forecast real GDP growth of 2%–3% in 2019, while the latest growth estimates by private-sector analysts averaged 2.3%. These projections were subject to the various uncertainties and risks discussed above. Local inflation edged up in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The slight rise in inflation partly reflected earlier growth in newly contracted private residential rentals. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years, total employment growth showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, local inflationary pressures were expected to remain moderate in 2019 as domestic economic growth momentum weakened. Following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and traded between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered four more times in March 2019 (as of 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid liquidity tightness. Moving into 2019, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, partly due to the rebuilding of carry trade positions. Despite the renewed triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. As a result of the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion as of 19 March. Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the three-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates rose by around 30 basis points to monthly averages of 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December. Moving into 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally declined as seasonal demand faded. The composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding cost, rose from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. In view of higher funding costs, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5–25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in late September. At the end of January 2019, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose in tandem with the Best Lending Rates to around 2.45%. Persistent uncertainties surrounding the China-US trade tensions and Brexit negotiations could heighten fund flow volatility. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates could stimulate arbitrage activities and lead to fund outflows. Under such circumstances, fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since the beginning of 2018, both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates had faced depreciation pressure amid market concerns over escalating China-US trade tensions. However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November amid optimism generated by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US. Despite the ongoing China-US trade tensions, there had so far been no significant impact on the funding position of the offshore interbank market. The overnight CNH HIBOR remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the three-month CNH HIBOR hovered at around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half, with renminbi customer deposits growing by 5.2% during the period. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high, rising further to RMB1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite concerns over the China-US trade tensions, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business was expected to continue expanding alongside the liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, the development of Stock Connect and Bond Connect, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. The local equity market experienced a roller-coaster ride over the past six months. At the beginning of the review period, the market fell sharply amid continued US monetary policy tightening, significant differences between the two sides in the China-US trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in the Mainland. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Fed shifted to a “patient” monetary policy stance. Meanwhile, during the trade war truce, China adopted further measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and open its markets to foreign investors. Despite the highly politicised legal action brought by the US against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides made conciliatory gestures, demonstrating their determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, the local equity market rallied sharply at the beginning of the year. However, considerable uncertainties remained as the two sides discussed the details of any agreement, while future developments in the US federal prosecution could complicate the situation, particularly in the high-technology sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew modestly last year. Yields declined, and performance improved towards the end of the year as market expectations of a slower pace of US monetary policy normalisation strengthened. As a result, bond fund flows reversed in the second half and recorded a modest increase. Issuance in Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi market rebounded sharply after declining for three consecutive years. However, as Mainland corporates continued to deleverage, total issuance remained below the amount of maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remained challenging, with its outlook hinging on economic developments globally and, in particular, in the Mainland.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but growth momentum weakened amid a combination of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly outside the US. In view of the dimmer growth outlook, the US Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be “data dependent” and that it would be “patient”, while removing its forward guidance on further rate hikes. As the US Fed’s policy inclination becomes data dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data and perceive monetary policy as becoming more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened global trade policy uncertainty and geopolitical risks may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have broadly stabilised since the end of 2018 amid signs of a pause in the US rate hike cycle and a stabilising US dollar. However, the region may face a broad-based slowdown amid a deteriorating external environment, namely the unresolved China-US trade conflict and weaker growth in advanced economies. In Mainland China, growth momentum moderated further in the second half of 2018, while uncertainty surrounding the growth outlook increased amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Policymakers therefore introduced more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. In the face of these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to prevent and control system-wide risks and supporting corporates and the real economy. The global economy continued to grow broadly in the second half of 2018. However, while the US economy remained generally solid, some signs of moderation emerged. There were also clear signs of weakening growth momentum outside the US. A number of country-specific shocks, including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new automobile emission standards in Germany, a surge in Italian Central Government bond yields amid a fiscal stand-off with the European Union, and social unrest in France, weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth posed headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp decline in oil prices in the fourth quarter also created new challenges for commodity-exporting emerging market economies. In view of the weakening growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth projection by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Indices for selected advanced economies Chart 2.2 Global import volume and industrial production in emerging market economies In the fourth quarter, slowing global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainty, market concerns over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, and the US Fed’s remarks that monetary policy would continue to tighten prompted a sharp correction in global equity markets. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to a degree not seen since the global financial crisis, raising concerns among some market participants that the US was approaching a recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread between 10-year and 3-month US Treasury yields and probability of a US recession Nevertheless, the probability of a US recession in the near term is low. US economic fundamentals remain solid, particularly the tight labour market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. Meanwhile, the US output gap is estimated to have turned positive only last year, and the likelihood of economic overheating prompting the US Fed to tighten monetary policy substantially is low. However, possibly taking into account the significant tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior US Fed officials began emphasising in early January that monetary policy would be data dependent, noting that moderate inflationary pressures allowed them to be “patient” in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its January meeting, the Federal Open Markets Committee removed its forward guidance on further rate hikes and announced that it “would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments”. This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) World ex USA Index and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the US Fed’s recent “dovish” signals, the US monetary policy outlook remains highly uncertain and depends on inflation and other developments. Moderate inflationary pressures thus far have given the US Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary policy normalisation. Inflation expectations have remained well anchored in recent years, supporting the case for patience (Chart 2.5). In addition, as US Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slower growth outside the US and trade policy uncertainty. In light of these developments, the US Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based measures of US inflation expectations However, the tight labour market is expected to continue supporting overall US economic performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which typically signals higher inflation ahead (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that have largely ruled out the possibility of a US Fed rate hike in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core personal consumption expenditure inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the Federal Funds target range remaining unchanged and of at least one rate hike in 2019 In summary, a prolonged pause in rate hikes by the US Fed is not a foregone conclusion. To reduce policy errors, the US Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data dependent as a risk-management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that could prompt monetary tightening. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also uncertain. In the Euro area, the ECB ended its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest in full the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance that policy rates would remain unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the ECB downgraded its near-term growth assessment in January, describing the risks surrounding the growth outlook as having “moved to the downside”. The implications of this downgrade to the ECB’s assessment of economic growth for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its latest policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid increasing downside risks. However, resistance to further monetary policy easing could be significant, given doubts over its effectiveness and the increasingly apparent drawbacks of a prolonged ultra-low interest rate environment. For example, as persistently low yields continued to weigh on profitability, regional banks’ capital ratios declined from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018. Therefore, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Apart from uncertainties surrounding the global monetary policy outlook, uncertainty over the outcome of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are two other major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. In early December, the US Government announced that it would refrain from raising tariffs on imports from China for 90 days and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the US and the European Union have made little progress at this stage. Uncertainty surrounding the outcome of these trade negotiations may continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the US, disagreements between the two parties over funding for border security resulted in a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democrat-controlled House of Representatives may lead to further policy gridlock. In the UK, risks related to Brexit and its knock-on effects surged after the May Government’s Brexit proposal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, and it remains uncertain whether a last-minute solution can be devised to avoid a disruptive “hard Brexit”. Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as the reimposition of US sanctions on Iran, may also create uncertainty over oil prices and thereby affect the global growth outlook. In East Asia, financial markets broadly stabilised in the fourth quarter after fluctuating during the first three quarters of last year. The stabilisation of the US dollar since October and signs that the US Fed would remain patient regarding further rate hikes eased currency depreciation and fund outflow pressures facing East Asian economies. Several regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio fund flows returned to a net inflow (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: Currency index and fund flows Despite financial market stability, there are increasing signs that the region may face a broad-based slowdown. As the China-US trade conflict weakened global trade momentum, export growth in the region declined, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to moderate in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-indices of the Purchasing Managers’ Indices for several regional economies, which indicate near-term external trade performance, have fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, suggesting that near-term growth momentum may weaken further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit Purchasing Managers’ Index new export orders indices for East Asian economies Amid slowing growth and the recent decline in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: Headline inflation rates and oil prices With recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar both remaining moderate, East Asian central banks have no urgent need to raise interest rates, easing the policy dilemma of balancing the promotion of economic growth against containing inflation and fund outflows. However, as private-sector debt in some East Asian economies remains high by emerging market standards, central banks continue to face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The Hong Kong economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower growth in private consumption and weaker export performance amid the China-US trade conflict. With global growth slowing, real GDP growth is also expected to moderate in 2019. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy and the performance of the Mainland economy. Local inflationary pressure should remain moderate in 2019, with the outlook subject to both upside and downside risks. Economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to maintain the strong momentum of the first half, with quarter-on-quarter GDP growth turning slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with growth in the fourth quarter coming in below trend at 1.3%, bringing full-year growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Based on the seasonally adjusted expenditure-based GDP volume index. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component The weakening of economic activity mainly reflected drags on consumption and exports from the direct or indirect effects of the China-US trade conflict. Private consumption growth moderated, possibly because of increased economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effect arising from the correction in local asset prices (Chart 3.1). Aggregate investment spending declined markedly amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong’s external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly after China and the US implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still contributed positively to GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance in greater detail and discusses its near-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Exports and imports in real terms As economic activity weakened, job growth appeared to slow in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to around 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, lower than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. Given weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly stable, with no signs of significant improvement. With global economic growth slowing further, Hong Kong’s economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. In the face of a challenging external environment, Hong Kong’s export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, although the low unemployment rate and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, private consumption growth is expected to moderate, partly reflecting weaker consumer confidence and the negative wealth effect arising from the earlier correction in asset prices. The outlook for fixed capital formation may become more uncertain. While building and construction activity is expected to maintain steady growth as housing supply increases, corporates may become more cautious about capital investment amid increased economic uncertainty. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers’ Index continued to hover in contractionary territory, and the index-based forecast of future economic growth points to a further slowdown in year-on-year GDP growth in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 2% to 3% in 2019, while the latest growth estimates by private-sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong’s growth outlook is subject to the various uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding two chapters. Although local inflationary pressure continued to build in recent months, it remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight increase in inflation momentum was driven by rises in certain services prices. Earlier growth in fresh-letting residential rentals and accelerated increases in the prices of meals out continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressure remained broadly moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). This mainly reflects weaker domestic growth momentum. However, the earlier rise in private residential rentals will continue to pass through to consumer price inflation. The market consensus forecasts a moderate headline inflation rate of 2.2% for the year, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation of 2.5%. The inflation outlook above is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, its lowest level in more than 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the currently near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if an easing of China-US trade tensions leads to better-than-expected performance by the local economy, local inflation may be pushed higher. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate The China-US trade conflict intensified progressively in the second half of 2018: on 6 July and 23 August, the US imposed additional tariffs of 25% on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from Mainland China respectively. Immediately following these two actions, Mainland China responded by imposing additional tariffs of 25% on an equivalent value of US goods. The US stepped up its actions on 24 September by imposing additional tariffs of 10% on US$200 billion worth of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing additional tariffs of 5% to 10% on US$60 billion worth of US goods. The two countries subsequently entered into negotiations to avoid further tariff hikes. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as an entrepôt between these two economies, the additional tariffs would inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through the trade channel. The China-US trade dispute therefore has important implications for Hong Kong’s macroeconomic and financial stability. This box reviews Hong Kong’s recent merchandise trade performance and discusses its near-term outlook. We also attempt to use more granular data to identify traded goods directly affected by the additional tariffs, thereby examining their impact in greater detail. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extract data on six groups of Hong Kong re-exports affected by the respective rounds of tariff hikes described in the preceding section. In the first two rounds of tariff hikes, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-finished goods, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment and energy equipment. In the third round, the range of affected goods was expanded to cover more consumer goods. For simplicity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of tariff hikes as List 1, List 2 and List 3 respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focus on year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong’s re-exports to adjust for seasonal effects. In addition, caution is warranted when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activity in that month was disrupted to some extent by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings in this section should be viewed only as preliminary evidence of the impact of the tariff hikes. Tariff-affected Hong Kong re-exports originating from the Mainland Shortly after the tariff hikes, the relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US through Hong Kong appear to have declined substantially or recorded slower growth (Chart B3.1). For example, growth in re-exports under Lists 1 and 2 slowed in the first month after the tariff hikes, while re-exports under List 3 recorded negative growth. Moreover, re-exports under all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US through Hong Kong in 2018 Tariff-affected Hong Kong re-exports originating from the US By contrast, goods re-exported from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports under List 1 appear to have declined substantially in the months following the tariff hikes, but recovered towards the end of the year. Re-exports under List 2 generally recorded negative growth throughout the year, while growth under List 3 appears to have remained broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong in 2018 Front-loading As there is sometimes a time lag between the announcement and eventual implementation of tariffs (or simply because of the threat of tariff hikes), corporates may increase shipments of affected goods before the expected effective date of the tariffs. Indeed, some information and news reports suggest that such front-loading was fairly common. Some private-sector analysts also considered such behaviour to be partly responsible for the strong headline trade figures before the tariff hikes. More granular trade data show some signs of front-loading for goods on certain tariff lists, but this appears to involve only goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). Growth in re-exports under Lists 1 and 2 increased in the months preceding the effective dates of their respective tariffs. On the other hand, growth in re-exports from the US to Mainland China through Hong Kong (Chart B3.2) does not indicate any apparent front-loading by corporates. Hong Kong re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports directly affected by the additional tariffs accounted for only around 4% to 5% of Hong Kong’s total re-exports by value. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong’s trade performance, re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs should also be examined. We find that re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs recorded negative growth in both of the final two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). In addition, the decline in growth of tariff-affected re-exports (red line) was visibly larger from the third quarter onwards, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in re-exports unaffected by the additional tariffs partly reflected a broader weakening in external demand. As persistent trade tensions increase uncertainty, global financial conditions tighten and geopolitical risks rise, external demand may come under more widespread pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has weighed on global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in the correction in major equity markets. This has in turn dampened import demand in other economies and constrained Hong Kong’s external trade performance. A likely slowdown in global growth in 2019 (see Chapter 2) is set to further constrain Hong Kong’s export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that corporates of all sizes are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trading sector particularly subdued. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades as liquidity tightened in anticipation of seasonal funding demand. Moving into 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, partly due to corporates repatriating proceeds from initial public offerings and the rebuilding of carry trade positions in the market, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates generally increased in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before declining in January 2019. Looking ahead, uncertainties arising from the ongoing China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation may lead to greater volatility in Hong Kong dollar fund flows. If the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential remains wide, carry trade activities may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and possibly triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and traded between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered four more times in March 2019 (up to 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity, but then gradually declined in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again from November onwards as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity and led to the unwinding of carry trades. Moving into 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporates repatriating proceeds from initial public offerings and the rebuilding of carry trade positions in the market. As the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential widened after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken gradually and triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance remained at around HK$76 billion from August onwards (Chart 4.2), before declining slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March (up to 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar funds that have flowed out since April 2018 represent only a small fraction of the approximately HK$1 trillion that has flowed in since 2008. Amid weak market sentiment and heightened equity market volatility, outflows from equity securities investment by Hong Kong residents accelerated, more than offsetting inflows from portfolio investment by non-residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). By contrast, debt securities investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, uncertainties arising from the ongoing China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation may heighten fund-flow volatility. In addition, the sizeable negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activities, resulting in fund outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered again. Fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Despite the ongoing normalisation of US interest rates and the repeated triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking from April to August, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year to HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base mainly reflected the decline in the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018 following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, Government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no notable change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (up to 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base As for broader measures of the Hong Kong dollar money supply, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) increased by 3.6% in the first half of the year but grew only slightly by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits were little changed compared with the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly due to fewer investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth amid higher deposit rates. An analysis of the asset counterparts shows that the slower growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 reflected changes in banks’ capital and reserves, which are included under “net other items”. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its asset counterparts Foreign currency deposit growth accelerated in the second half of the year. As banks attracted more deposits after raising preferential US dollar deposit rates, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half and became the main driver of growth in foreign currency deposits (Chart 4.6).
