Other foreign currency deposits increased slightly by 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Despite the continued sizeable Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base and deposit pool, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term interbank rates, causing them to be more volatile than longer-term interbank rates (Chart 4.7). The three-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, around 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Moving into 2019, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally declined as seasonal demand faded. The average three-month and 12-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downwards in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2018, the yields on three-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds declined by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, a measure of retail banks’ average Hong Kong dollar funding cost, increased slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before declining to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In view of higher funding costs, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5–25.0 basis points following the increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in September. However, retail banks did not further adjust their Best Lending Rates following another increase in the target range for the US federal funds rate in December. Meanwhile, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose in tandem with Best Lending Rates to around 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the US dollar interest rate path, fund flows and local financial market activities, such as initial public offering subscriptions, will continue to be the key drivers of Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Given that the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remains sizeable and the banking system holds a large amount of Exchange Fund Bills, which banks can use as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the Discount Window, the pace of increase in Hong Kong dollar interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of escalating China-US trade tensions, both the offshore renminbi and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened against the US dollar from the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November amid optimism arising from the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Thus far, the ongoing China-US trade tensions have not had a significant impact on funding conditions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before declining to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, possibly reflecting the monetary easing measures recently introduced by the People’s Bank of China. Nevertheless, the impact of progress in China-US trade negotiations on liquidity in the CNH interbank market in 2019 remains to be seen. Chart 4.10 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018, slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Among them, corporate customer deposits grew faster than personal customer deposits. However, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit declined further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced issuance of certificates of deposit and a relatively large amount of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Mainly due to higher net interest income, retail banks’ profit continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank rates and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalisation, retail banks’ overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs increased notably, but remained at a low level. Amid uncertainties in the external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth showed signs of stabilisation from November onwards, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds arising from the lingering uncertainties surrounding China-US trade relations, the global economic slowdown, uncertainty over the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant against the impact of a possible further deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate exposures. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets rose to 1.23% from 1.14% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly due to a significant increase in net interest income, which more than offset increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose to 1.27% from 1.16% in 2017. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period a year earlier (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and the decline in Hong Kong dollar interbank liquidity after the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in August 2018, Hong Kong dollar interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). Hong Kong dollar retail deposit rates also increased during the review period, as banks generally raised time deposit rates to compete for long-term stable funding. In addition, following the US interest rate hike decision in late September, banks raised their Best Lending Rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Reflecting higher wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) increased from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained low by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. More broadly, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to trend upwards. In the second half of 2018, banks’ average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs rose by 36 basis points, compared with an increase of 40 basis points in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks and term HIBOR The cumulative increase in HIBOR exceeded the rise in banks’ overall funding costs in Hong Kong, which may have had a positive impact on retail banks’ HIBOR-based mortgages, a type of loan that the industry had actively promoted over the preceding few years. However, further improvement in net interest margins may become more limited, as most HIBOR-based mortgages have reached their Best Lending Rate-based caps. Given the uncertainty over the timing of future increases in Best Lending Rates, the continued upward trend in banks’ funding costs amid US interest rate normalisation may weigh on overall net interest margins. Looking ahead, heightened uncertainties in the external environment may cloud banks’ profitability outlook. In particular, amid slowing global economic growth, lingering uncertainties surrounding China-US trade relations may dampen business sentiment and reduce demand for bank credit. If this results in a significant decline in lending and deterioration in asset quality, bank profitability may come under pressure. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and well above international minimum standards. At the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions increased further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated basis. 2. From 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with the figures up to December 2012. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a healthy level of 8.0% at the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions The liquidity position of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement, remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions increased from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also increased from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated stable funding positions among authorized institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained high at 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand a range of liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2018, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions edged up to 55.7% from 54.5% six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions 1. Figures may not add up to the total due to rounding. 2. Figures refer to percentages of total liabilities, including capital and reserves. 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances decreased during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions declined from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at year-end (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions declined from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. By contrast, as growth in Hong Kong dollar deposits was much lower than that in Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio edged up from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at year-end. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. It is estimated that, under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would decline by an amount equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at the end of 2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty over the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.11 Impact of an interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks 1. The interest rate shock refers to the impact of a standard parallel interest rate shock of 200 basis points on an institution’s interest rate risk exposure. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to its impact on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of the bank’s total capital base. Amid lingering uncertainties surrounding the China-US trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity and slowing global economic growth, credit growth decelerated significantly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth showed signs of stabilisation from November 2018 onwards. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018, after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline was attributable to slower growth in domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and a decrease in loans for use outside Hong Kong. Growth in domestic loans slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, growth in total lending slowed significantly to 4.4% from 16.1% in 2017. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Looking ahead, credit demand may remain weak in the near term. The HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2018 showed that, among all surveyed authorized institutions, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion expecting demand to decline increased to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite the slight decline in total lending in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of bank loan portfolios remained sound. The gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions edged down to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at the end of December 2018, from 0.61% and 0.40% respectively at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio edged down to 0.50%, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans edged up to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios were low by historical standards. Chart 5.13 Asset quality of retail banks 1. Classified loans are those loans graded as “substandard”, “doubtful” or “loss”. 2. Figures before December 2015 reflect the positions of retail banks’ Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. From December 2015 onwards, the coverage of the figures was expanded to include retail banks’ major overseas subsidiaries. On a half-yearly basis, growth in loans to households slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly attributable to slower growth in personal loans, including credit card advances and loans for other private purposes, which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong’s nominal GDP grew more slowly than loans to households, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak since early 2020 has dealt simultaneous blows to demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that differ from those of previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic shock from the pandemic, financial markets have remained volatile and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance staying stable and total deposits growing modestly, no notable outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After rebounding moderately in the first half of 2019, total lending growth slowed in the second half. The residential property market generally softened from mid-2019, albeit with some fluctuations. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued increases in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should carefully assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Global economic growth had shown initial signs of stabilisation since the fourth quarter of 2019, supported by stronger monetary easing by major central banks, easing China-US trade tensions and a reduced risk of a “no-deal Brexit”. However, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide since late January has sparked market concerns and triggered substantial volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks from the pandemic, several major central banks sharply reduced interest rates and expanded their liquidity facilities, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financial conditions tightened amid widening credit spreads and sharp equity market declines. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic will weigh on global economic activity, and the extent of its economic impact will depend on its severity and duration. Over the medium term, tensions between the US and its major trading partners may re-emerge, while the UK’s post-Brexit trade negotiations with the European Union may also encounter considerable difficulties. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia.1 East Asia’s exports to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, but whether there will be a broad-based rebound in the technology product cycle remains to be seen. Financial markets responded positively to the phase-one China-US trade agreement announced in December 2019, with the trade truce reducing global trade uncertainty to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel restrictions imposed by many economies in the region may weigh on Asia’s tourism industry, particularly in economies that are more dependent on tourism service exports. Given the region’s close supply-chain links with Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 amid weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the phase-one China-US trade agreement should temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressure remains amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 made economic stabilisation a priority for 2020, while also emphasising the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecast suggests that growth in the Mainland economy will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, the Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts pointed to a possible decline in the equity of private industrial enterprises in recent years, which was regarded as a sign of a “private-sector retreat”. Box 2 examines the drivers of changes in the equity of Mainland industrial enterprises using data on listed firms in 2018, and finds that private or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or “retreat”. Although the study finds that negative earnings are the largest driver, other factors, particularly structural factors, also warrant attention (see Box 2 for details). Local economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for 2019 as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Weaker domestic demand, particularly the contraction in private consumption, was the main drag on GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, resulting in a weak economic outlook that in turn dampened consumer and business sentiment. With China-US trade tensions escalating again, global economic growth slowing and inbound tourism deteriorating sharply, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained subdued. In view of the strong headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks more room to step up support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that it would reduce the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby allowing banks to release an additional HK$200 billion–HK$300 billion in lending capacity to corporates, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to be highly challenging, with the recent pandemic also posing significant downside risks. As the retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism and transport sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the pandemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020–21 Budget could provide assistance to households and corporates, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans to corporates with a 100% Government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.2 The HKMA’s further reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will give banks greater room to step up support for the local economy, especially sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure from the pandemic. In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment will likely remain weak amid fragile consumer and business sentiment. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the phase-one China-US trade agreement is expected to have a mildly positive impact on the local economy in the near term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while the growth forecasts of international institutions and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the global economic slowdown, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising and the real wage index falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the pandemic outbreak on the retail, accommodation and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate will rise further given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Box 3 discusses recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook in greater detail. Local inflationary pressure continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising prices of fresh pork; inflation momentum then gradually moderated as economic activity weakened. Inflation is expected to ease in the near term amid weak economic conditions, consolidating private residential rentals and moderate imported inflation. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation in 2020 to range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for Hong Kong dollars, including demand associated with initial public offerings, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened gradually from mid-October 2019. Moving into December, its upward momentum strengthened further, partly due to buoyant initial public offering activity and partly because liquidity tightness towards year-end prompted the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner during the review period, without triggering the Convertibility Undertakings. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates have fluctuated since the fourth quarter of 2019, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activity such as initial public offerings. Box 4 examines how market attention to upcoming initial public offering activity affects the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate rose gradually from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks’ continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the interest rate cap linked to their Best Lending Rates, the average lending rate for new mortgages increased to around 2.6% in October. However, as Best Lending Rates in the market were reduced from November onwards, the average lending rate for new mortgages edged down to around 2.5% by January 2020. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining strong, the Aggregate Balance staying stable and total deposits growing modestly, no notable outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, amid uncertainty in the external environment, we need to monitor the impact of any further deterioration in the coronavirus pandemic. With ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the ability, resources and determination to cope with fund outflows and maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. During the review period, the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened amid market expectations of a China-US trade agreement, but came under weakening pressure following the coronavirus outbreak from late January 2020. In the latter part of 2019, the offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi. Its discount widened temporarily at the end of January 2020, but the differential remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool rebounded slightly after a modest decline in the previous review period. The total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB637.4 billion at the end of January 2020. Hong Kong’s other renminbi business also expanded, with strong growth in renminbi bank lending and renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increased allocation to renminbi assets by international investors, and deeper regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising market hopes of a global economic recovery. However, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide since late January 2020 dashed hopes of a recovery, while growing investor concerns about a global economic downturn triggered a sell-off in global financial markets. To counter the economic shock, major central banks and some governments introduced stimulus measures from early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global growth outlook increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 clouded the outlook for regional economies. The coronavirus outbreak was expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the near term, with the tourism industry being particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asia continued to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage ratios. In Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 amid weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressure remained amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, while the authorities’ monetary and fiscal policy responses would provide some buffer. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainties, continued weakness in manufacturing and investment left global economic growth sluggish in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, economic growth showed initial signs of stabilisation in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly supported by the earlier policy easing by the Fed and the ECB, as well as an easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the China-US “Phase One” trade agreement. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index However, since the end of January, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide and the ensuing economic shock have raised market concerns and triggered a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in global supply chains, disruptions to production activity in the Mainland and the resulting drag on its economic growth would generate significant spillover effects that could spread across the world (Chart 2.3). Since late February, the surge in coronavirus infections outside Mainland China could further exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose the risk of a direct drag on domestic economic activity.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and option-adjusted spread of the Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services to Mainland China by selected major advanced economies in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP) To counter the potentially severe economic shock from the epidemic, some central banks, including the Fed, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England, cut interest rates from early March, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support households and corporates. Nevertheless, financial markets remained under immense selling pressure, resulting in a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which could in turn intensify downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economy Financial Conditions Index Apart from the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also clouded the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, although policy risks declined following the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations could be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remained unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the European Union and the United Kingdom were not expected to proceed smoothly, prolonging post-Brexit uncertainty. In addition, the sharp decline in oil prices since March would put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained sluggish in the second half of 2019 amid subdued global demand. The region’s exports to major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there were initial signs that the downturn in the regional technology cycle was bottoming out, including reports by major regional electronics companies of improved profits at the end of 2019,6 whether there would be a substantive rebound in regional technology exports remained to be seen. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), potentially affecting the region’s potential economic growth over the longer term. To support economic growth amid mild inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and South Korea lowered their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting them in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation The coronavirus outbreak raised concerns that regional economies could come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As many regional economies imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry bore the brunt of the impact, particularly in economies more reliant on Mainland Chinese visitors and tourism exports (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and worsening epidemic would also affect regional supply chains closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese visitors In the near term, the epidemic would continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Based on the experience of the SARS outbreak in 2003, these effects might be transitory, although the actual outcome would depend on the severity and geographical spread of the epidemic, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain it. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also faced multiple headwinds. First, despite market expectations that corporate earnings would deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions encouraged the search for yield, thereby driving up asset prices without support from fundamentals. As a result, regional equity markets became more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of constituents of benchmark equity indices Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth could make it more difficult for the region’s private sector to repay debt. Although lower domestic interest rates could provide some breathing space for indebted corporates and households, they could also sow the seeds of further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Box 1, the risk of debt accumulation in the private sector could be exacerbated as more index-tracking capital flows into regional financial markets, although this effect might be confined to the long-term borrowing of corporates with stronger financial fundamentals. Third, on the external front, East Asian economies could face increased risks from an increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress under the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, China-US trade tensions persisted as fundamental trade issues between the two countries remained unresolved. As evidenced by the widening trade surpluses of many regional economies with the US (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations might continue to seek alternative sources of supply outside China-centred supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies excluding China with the US had risen to approximately US$167 billion. If their trade surpluses with the US continued to widen, the Asian economies concerned could become the next targets of the trade conflict; for example, the US Government imposed hefty tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.7 In view of this, the regional trade outlook remained highly uncertain despite the China-US trade truce. Chart 2.9 Merchandise trade surpluses with the US Over the past decade, increased integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study showed that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows were driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices, commonly known as passive funds, but also actively managed funds that use investment indices as references.9 By bringing in overseas investors that the economies concerned would otherwise be unable to attract or access, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Such funds therefore diversify the investor base of emerging market economies, supporting long-term market growth and stability. But is there really such a thing as a free lunch? With regard to passive bond funds, there are concerns that their investments could weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers in which they invest, thereby resulting in high corporate leverage.10 In addition, it has been argued that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has increased the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors, more vulnerable.11 This box assesses the implications of index-driven investment for financial stability by examining these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to constituent bonds according to the weights of those bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions of passive bond funds could reduce the incentive for issuers of constituent bonds to act in the interests of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour could encourage excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and debt servicing risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies Using the weights of corporates from emerging market economies in a major index tracking corporate bonds of emerging market economies as a proxy for passive bond fund investment in their bonds,14 we find that an increase in such investment raises the long-term, rather than short-term, leverage ratios of the corporate issuers concerned. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 show the estimated effects. Apart from promoting the development of corporate bond markets in emerging market economies, the broader base of long-term bond investors created by passive bond funds also benefits the development of corporates in emerging market economies. We also find that the above effect is significant only for corporates in emerging market economies with stronger fundamentals, particularly those with stronger debt servicing ability and lower leverage ratios (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher costs of financial distress, corporates with high leverage or weaker debt servicing ability appear unlikely to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment. Overall, the above findings suggest that growth in passive bond fund investment may not substantially increase debt servicing risks in the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

The Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 amid weakening private consumption, reduced investment spending and poor export performance, entering recession for the first time since 2009. The economy is expected to face significant challenges in 2020, with the recent coronavirus outbreak posing a notable downside risk. The economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including slower global economic growth, China-US trade relations, economic performance in Mainland China and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate will likely rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease, although the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. The Hong Kong economy contracted visibly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the year as a whole, compared with growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since the Global Financial Crisis in 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed visibly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters, indicating that the economy had entered recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main drag on GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely disrupted consumption activities, while the weakening economic outlook undermined consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract visibly from the third quarter onwards. 33 Amid increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, aggregate investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter. 34 Externally, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained sluggish amid escalating China-US trade tensions, weakening global economic growth and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals into Hong Kong (Chart 3.2). 35 Affected by a sharp contraction in exports of services, net trade dragged down GDP in the third quarter, but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports Given the severe headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to ease the financial burden on the public, safeguard jobs and support corporates, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and severely affected sectors such as retail, food services, transport and tourism. 36 To give banks more room to step up their support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks would be reduced from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion–HK$300 billion to corporates, including SMEs. The Hong Kong economy is expected to face significant challenges in 2020, with the recent outbreak also posing a notable downside risk. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget could provide relief to households and corporates, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans with a 100% Government guarantee for corporates under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 37 The HKMA’s further reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will give banks more room to step up their support for the local economy, particularly sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the outbreak. Analysed by GDP component, private consumption and investment will likely remain weak amid fragile consumer and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the China-US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a mild positive impact on the local economy in the near term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the growth estimates by international institutions and private-sector analysts average -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in previous chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate increased from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and rose further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). In particular, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation and food services sectors rose to a nearly decade-high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year on year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly concentrated in the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year on year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, the labour market will continue to face greater challenges given the weak economic outlook described above, and the unemployment rate will likely rise further. Box 3 discusses in greater detail recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising prices of fresh pork, before inflation momentum gradually moderated as economic activity weakened. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying CCPI increased by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the increase easing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also softened from a peak of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The moderation in inflation momentum reflected reduced price pressures across various CPI components. For tradable goods, underlying food inflation remained visible due to higher fresh pork prices, although price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained moderate. For services, growth in the CPI rental component also trended down as growth in earlier fresh-letting private residential rentals moderated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures increased slightly but remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. Domestically, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rentals continue to moderate, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. Externally, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate amid weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. The market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2020 to range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5% and headline inflation at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a more severe-than-expected deterioration in the economy, for example due to a prolonged coronavirus outbreak, could further dampen inflation. On the other hand, more severe disruptions to the supply of fresh pork would exert upward pressure on inflation. Despite the visible slowdown in the Hong Kong economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%–2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It did not rise more visibly to 3.3% until the end of 2019 as the social incidents persisted. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this background, this box analyses recent labour market developments and the near-term outlook, including why the overall labour market remained generally resilient during the first three quarters of 2019, with the unemployment rate showing little change, and the implications for future developments. It also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs. Indeed, the unemployment rate tends to lag year-on-year real GDP growth by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature may explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real GDP growth and unemployment rate On the labour demand side, although China-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade sector and the retail- and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors continued to support the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the financial, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting declines in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economic recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained robust, while financial activities relating to fintech development and initial public offerings were also highly active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the financial and business services sectors. Moreover, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appeared less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, employment in the public administration, social and personal services sectors responds more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors even during an economic slowdown. Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019 On the labour supply side, the decline in the labour force participation rate40 from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019 provided a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various demand and supply factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bar) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 Meanwhile, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped contain the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted visibly in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, although employment declined during the economic downturn, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some changes in the structure of the labour market are also worth noting. In particular, the increasing share of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. Indeed, the shares of self-employed and underemployed persons in total employment have declined to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to increase, making them the second-largest group in total employment (around 7% in 2017). 42 Companies may therefore retain or employ more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have declined from a recent peak of 48 hours in 2010 to around 44 hours at present, partly reflecting the larger number of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened from October, with its upward momentum increasing further in December and keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range in recent months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar partly reflected equity-related demand and partly the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions amid liquidity tightness towards the year end. Overall, Hong Kong’s exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. Although the coronavirus outbreak could affect market sentiment and heighten volatility in fund flows amid an uncertain external environment, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding fund outflow pressures without compromising its financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar, including that arising from initial public offerings (IPOs), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October (Chart 4.1). Moving into December, its upward momentum increased further, with the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate staying on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range from mid-December to February. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate partly reflected buoyant IPO activity and partly the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions amid liquidity tightness towards the year end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) Broadly tracking movements in the US dollar, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER broadly followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.3 NEER and REER When measuring fund flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows and help assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Cross-border fund flows, on the other hand, focus on the geographical movement of funds through the banking system in Hong Kong and help assess the stability of Hong Kong’s overall financial system. The two concepts of fund flows require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the LERS, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA stands ready to purchase Hong Kong dollars at the request of banks, resulting in a reduction in the Aggregate Balance. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range in recent months. Therefore, no notable outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, total deposits in the banking system in Hong Kong are a useful indicator. If there is a large outflow from the banking system in Hong Kong, bank deposits will inevitably decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there was no notable cross-border fund outflow. Hong Kong’s exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner, suggesting that the coronavirus outbreak had only a limited impact on Hong Kong’s monetary environment. Nevertheless, the risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak need to be closely monitored. With ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to cope with fund outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. Despite the uncertain external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base remained sizeable, increasing by 4.0% from the end of June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. The other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and notes and coins in circulation issued by the Government, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base Broad Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators remained broadly stable during the review period. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) increased by 3.5% in the first half of 2019 and then edged up by 0.2% during the seven months since the end of June 2019. An analysis of the counterparts showed that the increase in Hong Kong dollar M3 since the end of June mainly reflected an increase in banks’ net foreign currency assets and an expansion in the Monetary Base arising from increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and notes and coins in circulation issued by the Government (Chart 4.5). Hong Kong dollar deposits, the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, remained broadly unchanged during the seven months since the end of June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterparts Foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% during the seven months since the end of June 2019 (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% over the period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits recording a slight decrease in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) grew steadily by 1.2% from the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong’s total broad money supply also increased at a relatively steady pace, with total M2 and M3 rising by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively from the end of June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand as well as business- and investment-related activities, the statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Aggregate broad money supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank rates fluctuated, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, as IPO activity in the Hong Kong equity market became more active, the overnight Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) experienced greater fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 Other short-term HIBORs generally increased during the review period. Subscriptions for large IPOs can exert significant pressure on the overnight rate. The empirical analysis in Box 4 shows that market attention to upcoming IPO activity also affects the three-month HIBOR. This may occur if market participants anticipate the future subscription deadlines of large IPOs and arrange medium-term funding in advance. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downwards in tandem with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on the three-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average new-mortgage lending rate On the retail front, the composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually increased from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. The increase mainly reflected banks’ continued raising of preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding, which drove up the weighted Hong Kong dollar deposit rate. Following the reduction in the target range for the US federal funds rate at the end of October 2019, a number of retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, retail banks’ Best Lending Rates currently ranged from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding housing loans, major banks raised the interest rate caps, which were set with reference to Best Lending Rates, on HIBOR-based mortgages. As a result, the average lending rate for new mortgages increased to around 2.63% in October. 45 Following the reduction in market Best Lending Rates from November, the average mortgage rate edged down to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to evolving risks to US economic activity posed by the coronavirus outbreak and to support the US Fed in achieving its policy objectives, the US Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). Although HIBORs track movements in US dollar interest rates over the longer term, short-term HIBORs may be affected by local factors that influence demand for the Hong Kong dollar, such as local IPO activity. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has declined since April 2018, HIBORs may have become more sensitive to changes in the supply of and demand for Hong Kong dollar funding. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong’s interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the event of short-term liquidity tightness, banks may use the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Amid concerns that the China-US trade conflict might intensify, both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates weakened notably in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Moving into October, market expectations of a resumption of China-US trade talks reversed the weakening trend of the renminbi. Both the offshore and onshore renminbi strengthened in the fourth quarter and briefly rose above 6.9 in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the phase one trade agreement between China and the US. However, since the end of January, both the offshore and onshore renminbi have again faced weakening pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. The offshore renminbi traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, but generally traded at a premium later in 2019. The discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, although the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the three-month CNH HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations in late August and late November due to MSCI’s A-share adjustments, and around the Lunar New Year holiday at the end of January 2020.

Amid increased uncertainties in the global and domestic economic environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined slightly in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although total loan growth moderated in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the review period. Accordingly, both the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions increased. However, given the stable level of the Aggregate Balance of the banking system and broadly stable deposits, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should carefully assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks59 declined slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, from 1.23% in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.2), their net interest income continued to register moderate growth during the review period. However, increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses resulted in a slight decline in profit. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite three 25-basis-point cuts in the US Fed Funds target rate in the second half of 2019, there has so far been no significant downward pressure in the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market. Instead, shorter-tenor Hong Kong dollar interbank rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019, reflecting various local factors, including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand arising from large initial public offerings and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market. Meanwhile, longer-tenor Hong Kong dollar interbank rates remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR standing at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to its level six months earlier (blue line in Chart 5.3). On the retail front, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts.60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding.61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at the end of 2019, although it remained low by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, as the decline in the US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding cost, their average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks’ net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding cost and the relatively high level of Hong Kong dollar interbank rates, supporting banking sector profitability over the same period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost and maturity have therefore been calculated as the weighted averages of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. As such, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and domestic environments will continue to cloud banks’ profitability outlook. These factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of China-US trade relations and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could further weaken the already sluggish momentum of global economic growth and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment may persist, which could put pressure on banks’ net interest margins going forward. Domestically, the local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and business confidence. Against an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or intensifies further, the outlook for credit demand and banks’ asset quality could deteriorate. In terms of overall market developments, the Hong Kong banking sector began launching virtual banking services following the issuance of eight virtual bank licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market shares by offering more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to acquire new customers, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the near-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited scale of virtual banks’ operations, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate their adoption of financial technology to remain competitive. The results in Box 5 show that the degree of financial technology adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically associated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above minimum international standards. At the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions increased further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also imposes a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)65, remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also increased moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio66, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, indicated that the funding positions of authorized institutions were stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand various liquidity shocks. At the end of 2019, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged, edging down from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Chart 5.9). Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, we estimate that the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would decline by an amount equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11).
