The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines brought hopes of economic reopening and boosted the global growth outlook. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets repeatedly reached new highs. Nevertheless, the global outlook remained clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery was expected to vary across economies. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels and the lasting economic scars of the pandemic would pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, mainly driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no sign of substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activity and subdued credit demand amid recurring outbreaks of the pandemic, total lending by the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, but still recorded a modest increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market was broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery and lingering geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment capability of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant against the impact of the relevant downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but slowed again as COVID-19 infections resurged from the fourth quarter onwards. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development at the end of 2020, market expectations that the pandemic would eventually come to an end were conducive to the global economy returning to normal and growth accelerating. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets reached new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this background, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. It remains to be seen whether vaccines can be distributed widely. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive policy easing may lead to higher-than-expected inflation, prompting central banks to scale back monetary easing earlier and bringing an end to financial markets’ expectations of a “lower for longer” monetary policy environment. Over the longer term, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the numerous economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and lasting economic scars. In East Asia, GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded and the search for yield re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia continued to face lingering uncertainties arising from the pandemic. First, amid global competition for vaccine procurement, the region’s less developed economies may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, uncertainties over vaccine supply, coverage or effectiveness, coupled with the weakened fiscal positions of governments in the region, may dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of fund flows. In Mainland China, the economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains highly dependent on developments in the pandemic and changes in China-US tensions. The latest consensus forecast projects the Mainland economy to grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi weakened for several months in early 2020, before strengthening during the remainder of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened and the Mainland bond market recorded strong capital inflows. A detailed study shows that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving fluctuations in the renminbi exchange rate (see Box 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level. With a modest increase in domestic demand and further expansion in merchandise exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to rebound in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed markedly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to around 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and, following a contraction of 1.2% in 2019, the first-ever decline for two consecutive years. The latest sectoral GDP data show that consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracted more sharply than the overall economy amid the pandemic. In response to the persistent pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund, the third and fourth rounds, in the second half of 2020 to assist sectors and members of the public affected by the pandemic and enhance Hong Kong’s anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the latest 2021-22 Budget to boost the economy, including the distribution of one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and the provision of 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for unemployed individuals. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year and an extension of the repayment period for trade financing loans under the Scheme. These extensions were expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines offered hope that economic activity would return to normal, and the local economy was expected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery were subject to numerous uncertainties, including developments in the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination would take time, the local economy would continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy was expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies would depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecast real GDP growth of 3.5%–5.5% in 2021, while the growth estimates of international organisations and private-sector analysts averaged 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate rose further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing employers with time-limited wage subsidies from June to November 2020 to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to sectors severely affected by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market was expected to remain under pressure amid weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Year-on-year underlying consumer price inflation declined markedly to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also remained low despite some fluctuations in recent months. As global and local economic conditions remained challenging, Hong Kong’s inflationary pressures were likely to remain mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation would continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in fresh-letting residential rental growth. The market consensus forecast headline inflation at a moderate 1.4% in 2021, while the Government forecast underlying and headline inflation rates of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including buoyant initial public offering activities and southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fundraising activity remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar strong. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in inflows of HK$263.3 billion into the Hong Kong dollar. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 85 times, resulting in cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. An analysis by geographical location showed that total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no sign of substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to developments in the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system and is therefore capable of withstanding volatility in fund flows. As the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking increased the Aggregate Balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank rates generally remained at very low levels. The composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. With lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also declined from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. Meanwhile, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Alongside the strengthening of the onshore renminbi (CNY), the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar from late May 2020 onwards. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium to its CNY counterpart, with the premium averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s CNH liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other renminbi business, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong declined, while renminbi trade settlement increased. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong has efficient financial infrastructure that provides investors with numerous cross-boundary channels for capital flows with the Mainland. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland’s capital account, growing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Supported by gains in global equity markets and active purchases of Hong Kong equities by Mainland investors through the Southbound Stock Connect, the local equity market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global equity markets rose on the back of unprecedented monetary easing by major economies, market optimism over positive progress in vaccine development that could help accelerate the recovery in economic activity, and reduced global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses after plunging in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period and briefly surpassing 31,000 points in mid-February 2021, a 32-month high. Supported by steady issuance, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi debt markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following substantial net outflows in the first half of 2020, bond fund inflows into the local market rebounded as business confidence recovered rapidly amid unprecedented economic stimulus measures introduced by governments worldwide. Despite a moderate rally in bond yields during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, continued to hover near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development raising market hopes that the COVID-19 pandemic would eventually end and global economic growth would accelerate, together with expectations of a “low-for-longer” global monetary policy environment, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic in late 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the disconnect between exuberant financial markets and the still-challenging macroeconomic environment could lead to asset price volatility if the economic recovery proves weaker than expected or policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, owing to higher-than-expected inflation). Looking ahead, policymakers face the difficult question of when to withdraw policy support and how to address the many legacies of the pandemic, including high debt levels and lasting economic scarring. Persistent uncertainty surrounding the pandemic continues to cloud the economic recovery in East Asia, with less-developed emerging market economies in the region likely to face greater challenges in procuring and distributing vaccines. Any setback in vaccination programmes could reverse the prevailing optimism and destabilise capital inflows and financial markets. In Mainland China, the economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the growth outlook remains highly uncertain, depending largely on the evolution of the pandemic and China-US tensions. The Government therefore announced that it would maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of containing system-wide risks. Benefiting from the release of purchasing power following economic re-opening, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, renewed increases in COVID-19 infections since the fourth quarter prompted governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, weakening global growth momentum again. The situation became more severe with the emergence of more transmissible variants in late 2020 and their subsequent spread around the world. Nevertheless, breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines in late 2020 raised market hopes that the pandemic would eventually end, allowing the global economy to normalise and growth to accelerate. Another source of support for the global economic recovery came from ongoing policy stimulus measures, including major central banks’ commitment to a “low-for-longer” monetary policy stance amid subdued inflation and continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) revised up its global GDP growth projection for 2021 to 5.5%, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 projection (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth projections by the IMF in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, improving market optimism and rising share prices in cyclical sectors that typically benefit from an economic recovery drove global equity prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major equity indices However, the disconnect between strong financial market performance and the still-challenging macroeconomic environment could lead to asset market volatility amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control depends on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX promote more equitable vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supplies are expected to make low vaccination rates a more acute problem in lower-income emerging market economies. If the pandemic is not brought under control as expected, social distancing and other restrictions may need to be extended, thereby undermining the global recovery outlook. Chart 2.3 Share of the population having received at least one vaccine dose in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the financial market rally has been underpinned by continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the “low-for-longer” monetary policy stance. However, there is a risk that support measures may be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing have already raised inflation expectations in the US and Europe (Chart 2.4). If inflation proves stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back monetary easing, while higher-than-expected inflation data could also increase financial market volatility. Chart 2.4 US and Euro area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates Third, the future course of China-US relations is subject to considerable uncertainty. The trend towards China-US “decoupling”, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish bipartisan stance towards Mainland China in the US, this trend may not reverse under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation in China-US tensions could trigger financial market turbulence. Looking ahead, policymakers will have to confront the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic-related support measures. While premature withdrawal could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a “cliff effect”, these measures are costly over the longer term, including the fiscal burden they impose and the delay they cause to the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources, such as by allowing “zombie firms” with no longer viable business models to survive through continued government support. In addition, policymakers will have to address the many legacies of the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 as corporate revenues declined and government spending surged (Chart 2.5). Although the problems arising from the rapid increase in debt may not be imminent given the current extremely low level of global interest rates, continued debt accumulation by both the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt-to-GDP ratio Another legacy concerns the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty may prompt corporates to reduce investment, while workers experiencing prolonged unemployment may permanently leave the labour market, resulting in a substantial waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after plunging in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The economic recovery was mainly driven by a rebound in exports, with particularly strong export demand for electronics and technology equipment. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit service sectors, such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact with customers, remained under strain. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite continued uncertainty surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio capital inflows resumed. Since the second half of last year, improving market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced economy bonds have attracted stronger bond fund inflows into the region (Chart 2.7). Equity fund inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020 amid signs of economic recovery and the rollout of vaccine production programmes. Regional currencies appreciated accordingly on portfolio capital inflows, with the Bloomberg-JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding by around 10% from its trough in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio capital flows East Asia continues to face persistent uncertainty surrounding the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines offers hope to the region’s hard-hit service sectors and economies, global competition for early vaccine supplies has raised procurement costs, while vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region’s logistics and public health capacities. As a result, less-developed economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, while uneven vaccination across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, as investor optimism has been driven largely by the vaccine rollout, the current capital inflows and rally in financial asset prices could end if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls far short of expectations. An abrupt decline in capital inflows could trigger another bout of market turbulence. With COVID-19 successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports continued to grow on strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical supplies and high-tech products (Chart 2.8). For 2020 as a whole, Mainland GDP still grew by 2.3% despite the unprecedented shock from the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contribution to GDP growth by demand component Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts suggest that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery can be sustained will still depend partly on the evolution of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland have normalised, the service sector remained somewhat disrupted amid renewed outbreaks in several northern provinces. On the external front, despite a return to export growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remained uncertain amid fresh waves of the pandemic in most developed economies. In addition, China-US tensions may not ease in the near term. Nevertheless, the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the agreement reached on the EU-China Comprehensive Agreement on Investment should facilitate Mainland China’s further integration with other economies, potentially offsetting some of the adverse impact of China-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Given the continued uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook, the Government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not change significantly in 2021 in order to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of containing system-wide risks, such as maintaining stable macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. Over the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan identifies technological self-reliance and the dual-circulation strategy as development priorities, with the aim of bringing per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The COVID-19 outbreak appeared to have had only a limited impact on the repayment capability of bond-issuing corporates, with the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remaining low in the second half of 2020. However, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 due to a sharp rise in defaults on state-owned enterprise bonds (Chart 2.9). While the increase in SOE defaults mainly reflected the Central Government’s determination to break implicit guarantees for SOEs and promote more rational market pricing of risks, constrained fiscal space among some local governments, particularly those in less-developed regions, may also have been a contributing factor. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Amount and ratio of onshore bond defaults Funding costs for corporate issuers increased in the second half of 2020, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the ongoing economic recovery and gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to higher funding costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate defaults in the final quarter of 2020 led to a notable widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields In the property market, Mainland housing prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. By contrast, housing prices in lower-tier cities increased at a much slower pace (Chart 2.11). The housing oversupply problem that had troubled third-tier cities in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because third-tier cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. By the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained at around 13 months, well below its peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real GDP remained far below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 as domestic demand picked up and merchandise exports expanded further. With COVID-19 vaccination raising hopes that economic activities would return to normal, the Hong Kong economy is expected to resume growth in 2021 after recording its most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine roll-outs. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the Hong Kong economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. The labour market is therefore expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflationary pressures should stay mild. The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activities remained far below their pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and marked the first consecutive annual contractions in history following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry also showed that economic activities in the vast majority of industries recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related industries contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to rebound in the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Domestic private consumption resumed positive growth in the third and fourth quarters. However, consumer confidence remained weak as the authorities reimposed social distancing measures amid the third and fourth waves of the local epidemic. Aggregate investment spending also increased in the second half of the year as business sentiment briefly improved. Partly benefiting from stronger export performance, particularly exports to Mainland China, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as global tourism was still at a standstill. Overall, net imports (the trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting a slower rebound in merchandise exports than imports. In the latest 2021/22 Budget, the Government also announced additional countercyclical measures to boost the economy, including the distribution of one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and the provision of a 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for the unemployed. In March 2021, the HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced a further extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, as well as an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash-flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to enable economic activities to return to normal, the Hong Kong economy is projected to resume positive growth in 2021 as a whole, although the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine roll-outs. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further and provide support to Hong Kong’s exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their mass vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong’s merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for the whole of 2021 in the range of 3.5%–5.5%, while the growth estimates by international organisations and private-sector analysts average 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021 (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS outbreak. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while Government figures showed that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The year-on-year growth of the Nominal Index of Payroll per Person Engaged, a measure of labour earnings, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide employers with time-limited wage subsidies from June to November 2020 to help them retain employees. Following the completion of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures, such as one-off subsidies, under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide further support to industries hard hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure given weak economic conditions. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. On a year-on-year basis, underlying consumer price inflation fell markedly to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also remained low in recent months despite some slight fluctuations. Specifically, price pressures on basic foodstuffs eased, while the cost of meals out declined visibly, reflecting the takeaway discounts offered by more restaurants when dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures on other tradable goods, such as durable goods, remained moderate. On the services front, the CCPI rental component remained soft as private housing rentals consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). In particular, local inflation will continue to be contained by the earlier moderation in fresh-letting residential rental growth. The market consensus forecasts a moderate headline inflation rate of 1.4% for 2021, while the Government forecasts underlying and headline inflation rates of 1% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism rapidly fell into a slump, raising concerns that the crisis could have a scarring effect on the subsequent labour market recovery. Against this background, this box empirically analyses the impact of a boom in inbound tourism on Hong Kong’s labour market to shed light on the potential impact of the current tourism slump. Inbound tourism has experienced significant ups and downs since 2000 (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Visitor arrivals began to surge following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year. Under the original IVS, Mainland residents could apply to visit Hong Kong individually once or twice a year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded in April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry individual visit endorsements to Hong Kong valid for one year. Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure links with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached record highs between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, while inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020 amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies Taking the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We consider the launch of the IVS in 2003 to be akin to a random economic shock because its timing was nearly exogenous and its introduction could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. The main data for our analysis are population data from Hong Kong’s Population Census or Population By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Census or Population By-census. We also define tourism-related industries as the catering, retail, hotel and transport industries. First, we adopt a difference-in-differences analytical framework to compare differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers aged 20–40 in the treatment group and older workers aged 41–65 in the comparison group. We classify the younger cohort as the treatment group because they are still at an early stage of their careers and can make major changes to their employment choices more flexibly in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the labour market impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS may vary over time, we also use an event study to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical findings show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers, particularly women and those with only secondary education, were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the IVS had a particularly significant and persistent impact on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries, remaining close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards in terms of the average difference in the probability of entering such industries relative to the older cohort (Chart B2.2). Using a similar approach, we also compare the earnings of workers in tourism-related industries (the treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (the comparison group). The estimation results show that, following the implementation of the IVS, earnings growth among workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that among employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and workers with lower educational attainment in tourism-related industries recorded higher and rising earnings growth of 3–20 percentage points (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the earnings of female workers and workers with lower educational attainment The above findings are broadly consistent with international experience, showing that the tourism industry is an important source of employment, particularly for young people, women and workers with lower educational attainment. In Hong Kong’s case, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses showing that strong growth in inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and enhanced the resilience of the labour market for lower-skilled workers. As inbound tourism has fallen from boom to bust, these groups of workers may be more adversely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU), with the strong-side CU being triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant IPO fundraising activities and southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) declined across the board. Although uncertainties surrounding the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and is capable of withstanding the pressure arising from volatility in fund flows. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side CU, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that arising from buoyant IPO fundraising activities and southbound fund inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some of the proceeds raised through IPOs were remitted out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505–7.7544 in November and December amid stronger sentiment in the local equity market and market expectation of increased funding demand towards the year-end. With fundraising activities remaining buoyant in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the Aggregate Balance increased as the strong-side CU was triggered multiple times, reflecting substantial fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. The strong-side CU was triggered 47 times between September and October 2020. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side CU was triggered 85 times in total during 2020, with cumulative inflows amounting to HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, suggesting no sign of substantial fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any unusual fund movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) declined, broadly tracking the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had only a limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the REER broadly followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery and persistent China-US tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities, such as IPOs, resulting in substantial fund inflows into and outflows from Hong Kong. On the one hand, such fundraising activities may attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, the proceeds raised by listed firms may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business purposes. With ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, Hong Kong is capable of withstanding volatility in fund flows without compromising financial stability. Amid continued fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 20.8% in the eight months since the end of June 2020 (Chart 4.5). Analysed by component, the increase in the Monetary Base during the period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance resulting from the multiple triggering of the strong-side CU. Meanwhile, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, Government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO fundraising activities increased Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, resulting in notable increases in Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component from July to October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the completion of IPO fundraising activities and customers’ repayment of IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Moving into January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased sharply again, mainly driven by large-scale IPO fundraising activities at the end of January. Overall, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased by 21.7% in the seven-month period since the end of June, or by a moderate 9.1% after excluding the impact of the end-January IPO fundraising activities. An analysis of counterpart assets shows that, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the Monetary Base resulting from the triggering of the strong-side CU (Chart 4.7). As the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 22.9% during the same period, or by a moderate 9.1% after excluding the impact of the end-January IPO fundraising activities. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits declined amid low deposit rates, the decrease was fully offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% in the seven-month period since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weak US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% during the same period, mainly reflecting the increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, owing to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO fundraising activities, total deposits with authorized institutions rose sharply by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the end-January IPO fundraising activities, total deposits increased moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may be volatile owing to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand as well as business- and investment-related activities, and should therefore be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance, HIBORs generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale IPO fundraising activities in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not fluctuate significantly owing to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly followed the movement of the US dollar yield curve and steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government bond yields, composite interest rate and average new-mortgage lending rate At the retail level, Hong Kong dollar interest rates generally declined in tandem with HIBORs. The composite interest rate, a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, declined further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). With lower funding costs, the average new-mortgage lending rate also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the one-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, retail banks’ Best Lending Rates remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the LERS, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low US interest rate environment, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should remain low, with occasional fluctuations arising from capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong’s monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from the end of May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the more favourable economic outlook for Mainland China compared with the rest of the world, as well as the weak US dollar. FTSE Russell’s announcement at the end of September that Mainland Central Government bonds would be included in the World Government Bond Index further supported the strengthening of the renminbi through investment demand. During most of the review period, the CNH traded at a premium to the CNY, with the premium averaging around 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the CNH interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations owing to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards the year-end, it stayed below 4% most of the time (Chart 4.11). The three-month CNH HIBOR declined in late December in tandem with onshore renminbi interest rates, before rising again in late January, partly owing to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Renminbi deposits grew at a faster pace from the fourth quarter onwards, partly reflecting renminbi appreciation and higher renminbi interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a faster pace, rising by 21.9% to RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021 (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Of the total, renminbi customer deposits increased by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong As for other renminbi business, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion in the seven-month period from the end of June 2020. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow strongly. During the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, representing an increase of 16.7% from the same period a year earlier. Among these transactions, outward remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland increased faster than inward remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong’s deep renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. For 2020 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Amid a prolonged economic downturn caused by the recurring COVID-19 pandemic and the prolonged low interest rate environment, profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined further in the second half of 2020, while their asset quality also deteriorated slightly. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient, underpinned by its strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA decided to extend various relief measures to continue supporting the overall economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic will be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. These uncertainties and lingering geopolitical tensions would weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic would weaken the repayment capability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of the related downside risk factors on its asset quality. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 38.5% in the second half of 2020 compared with the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets fell to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed to 1.01% in the second half of 2020 from 1.63% in the same period in 2019 (Chart 5.2), reducing net interest income by an amount that more than offset the modest increase in non-interest income and resulting in lower profits. For 2020 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 29.4%, while the return on assets fell to 0.77% from 1.19% in 2019. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely reflecting substantial fund inflows driven by equity market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant. HIBORs softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month HIBOR decreased by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) showed a broadly similar movement, declining notably from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates More broadly, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong declined moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks’ net interest margins. In addition, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the path of economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the banking sector’s loan quality and profitability in the near term. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a healthy level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratios under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirement also indicated stable funding positions of AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of AIs suggest that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits continued to be the primary source of funding for AIs, reflecting the stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all AIs, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all AIs As total deposits with all AIs increased in the second half of 2020 while total lending declined over the same period, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Accordingly, the average Hong Kong dollar and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratios declined to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively at the end of 2020, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a hypothetical shock of an across-the-board 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions is estimated to decline by an amount equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks Against the backdrop of a prolonged economic downturn caused by the recurring pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances recorded a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, for 2020 as a whole, total bank credit still recorded positive growth, although the growth rate slowed markedly to 1.2% from 6.7% in 2019. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all AIs decreased by 1.8% in the second half of 2020 after increasing by 3.0% in the first half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total lending was attributable to decreases in both domestic loans (comprising loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Specifically, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, after growing by 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans remained broadly unchanged at the end of 2020 compared with the end of June, after declining by 2.0% in the first half. Foreign currency loans decreased by 4.5% in the second half of 2020 after rising sharply by 10.6% in the first half, partly reflecting weaker demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. Banks became slightly more optimistic about the near-term credit demand outlook compared with six months earlier. According to the HKMA Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2020, the share of surveyed AIs expecting loan demand to increase in the next three months rose to 37%, while the share expecting loan demand to decline over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment capability of households and corporates, banks’ loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross classified loan ratio of all AIs rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the gross classified loan ratio and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economy weakened, while inflationary pressures continued to intensify worldwide, particularly in the US. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale COVID-19 outbreaks and the possibility of greater-than-expected monetary tightening if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than expected. If the US Fed tightens monetary policy substantially and causes global financial conditions to tighten, the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies (EMEs) would come under pressure. More recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could have significant implications for the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits increased moderately during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, growth in total bank lending accelerated. Meanwhile, the residential property market softened from mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the ongoing economic recovery. Together with the possibility of a faster-than-expected normalisation of US monetary policy, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impacts of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness extending into 2022, as the spread of the highly transmissible Omicron variant led to increased mobility restrictions worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and became broad-based across goods and services in major advanced economies (AEs), particularly the US. More recently, following the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the surge in commodity prices could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility might lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties. In the near term, renewed lockdowns and a further deterioration in supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out in the event of large-scale COVID-19 outbreaks. In the US, as the risk of inflation proving more persistent and broad-based than expected increased, the US Fed turned more hawkish, accelerating the timetable for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet. If the US Fed needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financial conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers’ debt servicing ability, while disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable EMEs. More recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may expose global commodity prices to the risk of sustained increases, exacerbate shortages in industrial supplies and heighten financial market volatility. Increased market volatility may also trigger redemption pressure on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds, can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the momentum temporarily slowed as some Southeast Asian economies reimposed stringent COVID-19 restrictions in the third quarter, while regional exporters of technology products, namely South Korea and Singapore, continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although emerging Asia is widely expected to see a broad-based recovery in 2022, the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, particularly for regional economies with lower vaccination rates and constrained public healthcare resources. Second, the US Fed’s accelerated policy normalisation may trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressure. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support their economic recovery will face a more difficult trade-off between containing capital outflow pressure and supporting economic activity. Third, the slowdown in major economies, coupled with a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the trade growth outlook. Fourth, increases in various commodity prices triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will feed through to regional inflation while weakening consumption. Together with heightened global economic uncertainty, this will further complicate regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. Over the longer term, to rebuild a sustainable and resilient growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is affected by corporate environmental performance. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term amid the persistent property market downturn and Omicron outbreaks. Accordingly, the Mainland authorities made stabilising growth their top priority for the year and introduced a series of supportive fiscal and monetary measures. The total amount of onshore bond defaults and onshore bond defaults by state-owned enterprises both declined in the second half of 2021. Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risk in the banking sector remained manageable, as Mainland banks, particularly systemically important banks, had limited exposure to loans to property developers, low NPL ratios and high provision coverage ratios. Hong Kong’s economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew moderately as merchandise exports and private consumption benefited from the ongoing global economic recovery, improving local labour market conditions and the Government’s launch of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full year of positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local COVID-19 infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures weighed on local economic activity. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flows, the 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme (SFGS) would be enhanced, with their maximum loan amounts increased and their application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also offered borrowers a one-year partial principal repayment option, which was also applicable to loans under the SFGS. Hong Kong’s economy is expected to continue recovering in 2022 as a whole, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global growth amid the lingering pandemic and a higher base effect. In particular, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from the expansion of the global economy. The Government’s promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 2.0%–3.5% in 2022, while the growth forecasts of international organisations and private-sector analysts average 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to the uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding sections, particularly those relating to the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining to 3.9% at year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressure had re-emerged amid a new wave of local COVID-19 infections. In addition, the decline in online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local infections and tightened COVID-19 restrictions will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on developments in the local pandemic situation and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures generally increased in recent months but remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also picked up in recent months, partly owing to increases in the prices of meals out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-induced logistics disruptions. However, soft rentals and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecast for the headline inflation rate in 2022 is 2.4%, while the Government projects the headline and underlying inflation rates for 2022 at 2.1% and 2.0% respectively. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar had gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market. Although the Hong Kong dollar rallied slightly at one point in October 2021, its strengthening momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connects and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen alongside the US Fed’s monetary policy normalisation. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone most of the time and continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits increased moderately during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Amid ample interbank liquidity, HIBORs remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Offshore renminbi banking business continued to flourish. In particular, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand, with the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022. Although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans declined, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system increased to RMB1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from Hong Kong’s efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, as well as the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increased demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Supported by monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, the global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global equity markets generally higher in the final quarter of 2021, propelling the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, sharply rising commodity prices and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict led major global equity markets to consolidate from early January 2022.

The global economy slowed visibly in late 2021 amid the rapid worldwide spread of the COVID-19 variants (Delta and Omicron) and persistent production bottlenecks, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and became broad-based across goods and services in major advanced economies (AEs), particularly the US. Rising inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the US Fed’s monetary policy stance, heightening the risk that premature tightening of global financial conditions could put the currently elevated asset valuations under pressure and weigh on emerging markets, where recoveries generally remained behind the curve. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered global financial market volatility, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant across the region, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with the region’s major technology-product-exporting economies continuing to outperform other economies. While the Omicron variant is unlikely to seriously derail the region’s economic recovery, any uncertainty associated with new variants will continue to cloud the economic outlook for the region. In addition, US Fed policy normalisation could trigger corrections in regional asset prices, while slower growth in major economies could weigh on the region’s growth in goods exports. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, has led to higher commodity prices and increased inflation risks and, on the other hand, will weaken consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, complicating regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021 amid a resurgence of COVID-19 infections, power rationing and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from the cooling property market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the Government has made stabilising growth its top priority for the year, while macroeconomic policies will also provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed visibly in the final quarter of 2021 as the highly transmissible Omicron variant spread on top of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tightened mobility restrictions around the world. In addition, supply chain problems, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs including semiconductors, continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the US and other major AEs, and slower growth momentum in Mainland China, which offset the expected growth rebound in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF projections of real GDP growth Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose visibly in major AEs, particularly in the US, where larger-scale policy stimulus had been implemented since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, the release of pent-up demand and labour shortages, inflationary pressures became broad-based across goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up the prices of various commodities and may exacerbate the already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core consumer price index inflation rates in selected economies (1) The latest data for the US, the UK and the Euro area are for January 2022, while those for the remaining economies are for December 2021. (2) “Asian advanced economies” include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) “Asian emerging market economies” include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook is subject to significant uncertainties with downside risks tilted to the downside, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how the impact of geopolitical tensions on global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment evolves, and major central banks’ policy responses to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have so far responded to the recent surge in Omicron cases with targeted measures focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote working and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these less stringent measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown initial signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, in the event of large-scale outbreaks, the reimposition of lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which could lead to a renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers’ Index – suppliers’ delivery times sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to ease gradually, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current elevated global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia will push up commodity prices, the lagged pass-through of higher production costs to final selling prices, the possibility that the earlier surge in global residential property prices will drive up rentals going forward, upside risks to wage growth from tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the US Fed shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at the Federal Open Market Committee meeting in December 2021, dropping its characterisation of high inflation as “transitory”, doubling the pace of asset purchase tapering from US$15 billion to US$30 billion per month with a view to ending the asset purchase programme by March 2022, and beginning discussions on reducing its balance sheet.
