Indeed, recent market pricing indicated that the US Fed might raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. By contrast, given the Euro area’s closer trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, the ECB may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this background, coupled with persistently elevated global debt levels and asset valuations under prolonged policy accommodation, if persistent inflationary pressures require the US Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, borrowers’ debt servicing ability could be at risk of deterioration and financial market volatility could be triggered. More recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe intensified, risk aversion in financial markets increased and signs of US dollar shortages emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. Amid premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Increased market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on OEFs, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing, a liquidity management tool for OEFs, can reduce these funds’ liquidity risk during periods of market stress, as well as the tool’s potential limitations. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as the region’s major exporters of technology products, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the unevenness of recoveries across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures remained moderate in many emerging Asian economies. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index Emerging Asia is generally expected to see a broad-based recovery in 2022, but the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread across the region since late 2021, its economic impact has remained milder than that of previous waves of infections. However, some regional economies where vaccination rates remain behind and public health resources are more constrained will continue to face the threat of new variants. Second, US Fed policy normalisation could trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support their economic recoveries will face a more difficult trade-off between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, given their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden surge in long-term US yields could also spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, increasing the risk of corrections in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian 10-year sovereign bond yields and corresponding US Treasury yields Third, the outlook for the region’s goods trade is subject to uncertainties arising from slower growth in major economies and a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, which could weaken the region’s export growth. Chart 2.6 US: Imports from emerging Asia and real GDP Fourth, although regional economies have relatively limited trade and financial links with Russia and Ukraine, higher commodity prices arising from the conflict will pass through to regional inflation while weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, this will complicate regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also alerted regional economies to the long-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in preparation for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to attach greater importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether equity market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporates’ environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a major shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some OEFs experienced substantial fund outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Fund outflows from selected OEFs during the March 2020 episode In addition to investors’ liquidity needs, another possible reason for the substantial fund outflows was investors’ “first-mover advantage” in redeeming funds early, thereby avoiding redemption costs that could surge during periods of market stress. To curb fund outflows arising from the first-mover advantage, some OEFs employ swing pricing—an OEF pricing rule that reduces investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many OEFs used swing pricing during this episode, there has been no empirical research showing whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from OEFs. Against this background, this box conducts an empirical study to determine whether swing pricing reduced fund outflows from OEFs during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. In addition, this box seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we offer policy recommendations from a financial stability perspective. First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing redemption costs on to them. First-mover advantage mainly exists in OEFs that adopt conventional pricing rules, under which the subscription and redemption costs incurred by fund investors, such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments, are reflected in OEF prices only after transactions are executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not need to bear these transaction costs. This gives them an incentive to redeem their fund holdings early, particularly when substantial redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during periods of market stress, first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced because redemption costs are expected to rise. This increases the redemption pressures and liquidity risk faced by OEFs.

With merchandise exports and private consumption continuing to grow, the Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, resuming positive growth for the full year for the first time since 2019. Moving into 2022, a new wave of the local epidemic and the resultant tightening of social distancing measures exerted pressure on local economic activities. The overall economy is expected to continue its recovery in 2022 as a whole, although the strength and pace of the recovery will be subject to uncertainties and risks arising from the epidemic and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These headwinds may also affect the labour market outlook following its notable improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up in the near term alongside rising import prices, soft local rentals and labour costs should contain overall price pressures. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), although the pace of growth moderated compared with the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activities grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). Domestically, private consumption increased amid improving labour market conditions and the Government’s implementation of the Consumption Voucher Scheme. However, aggregate investment spending declined in the final quarter following strong rebounds in the preceding two consecutive quarters. Externally, Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance remained robust alongside the ongoing global economic recovery, while trade in services remained weak, partly because inbound tourism was still at a standstill (Chart 3.2). On a net basis, external trade was a drag on GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volume A new wave of the local epidemic and the resultant tightening of social distancing measures exerted pressure on local economic activities in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the Special 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme would be enhanced, with their maximum loan amounts increased and their application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The Scheme also offered borrowers a one-year partial principal repayment option, which was also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue its recovery in 2022 as a whole, although the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global economic growth amid the lingering pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from the expansion of the global economy. The Government’s promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2022 in the range of 2.0% to 3.5%, while the growth estimates by international organisations and private-sector analysts average 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong’s economic recovery are subject to the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in previous chapters. In particular, recent epidemic developments, the faster pace of US monetary policy normalisation and heightened geopolitical concerns, such as the Russia-Ukraine situation, have clouded the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the global economy. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China could stimulate local economic growth. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining to 3.9% at the end of the year (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, albeit still below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data suggested that pressure on the labour market had re-emerged amid a new wave of the local epidemic. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also indicated fewer new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of the local epidemic and tightened anti-epidemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly on sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local epidemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). Inflation momentum, as measured by the annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, also picked up in recent months. Specifically, prices of meals out and certain energy-related items rose at a faster pace amid the recovery in local demand and rising external prices (Chart 3.5). Meanwhile, the CCPI rental component continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Real unit labour costs remained soft but edged up in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average salaries (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Hong Kong’s import prices Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.7 Unit labour cost Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-related disruptions to logistics. However, soft rentals and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. The market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2022 to reach 2.4%, while the Government forecasts the headline inflation rate at 2.1% and the underlying inflation rate at 2.0% for 2022.

Amid risk aversion in the local stock market and concerns over the normalisation of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. With ample Hong Kong dollar liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates continued to stay low. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Looking ahead, while uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system and is capable of withstanding the shocks arising from volatility in fund flows. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking zone most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar had gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rallied slightly in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, its strength subsequently lost momentum, mainly due to weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations of a stronger US dollar amid an increasingly hawkish US Fed monetary policy outlook. IPO fundraising activities continued to provide support to the Hong Kong dollar during the review period (Chart 4.3). Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no notable sign of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance-of-payments statistics showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no sign of unusual cross-border fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) remained stable due to the appreciation of the renminbi against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) generally followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.4 NEER and REER Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, developments in the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund-flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds, the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions, could cause the Hong Kong dollar to weaken and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking as part of the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS). Hong Kong also has ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system and is capable of withstanding volatility in fund flows without compromising financial stability. Hong Kong’s monetary environment stayed accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base increased by 1.4% in the eight months since the end of June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional issuance to meet banks’ continued demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion during the review period to HK$1,188.7 billion, with the Aggregate Balance before Discount Window activities decreasing correspondingly by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits with authorized institutions increased modestly by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics are subject to volatility due to a wide range of transient factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering (IPO)-related funding demand as well as business- and investment-related activities. It is therefore more appropriate to observe the longer-term trends. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency Overall, Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Given the ample liquidity in the banking system, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates continued to stay low despite market concerns over US monetary tightening (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of higher funding demand towards the year end, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates edged up in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages edged up from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. Meanwhile, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, the ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer during large-scale capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates During the review period, the offshore renminbi (CNH) interbank market continued to function normally. Amid seasonal liquidity demand towards the year end, the overnight CNH HIBOR fluctuated slightly in late December 2021, while the three-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable and hovered around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. During the six months since the end of July 2021, the total outstanding amount of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased by 30.3% to RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among the total, renminbi customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in the outstanding amount of certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9 Renminbi deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong During the six months since July 2021, while the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, Hong Kong’s renminbi trade settlement continued to grow. Transactions handled by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,763.0 billion between the end of July 2021 and the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.10), representing an increase of 18.3% from RMB3,181.0 billion during the same period a year earlier. The deep renminbi liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to support a large volume of renminbi payments and financing transactions. For 2021 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system increased from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Flows of renminbi trade settlement payments Looking ahead, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the establishment of the two-way Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continuing liberalisation of the Mainland’s capital account, increased demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Major global equity markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but consolidated from January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong equity market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly weighed down by sharp declines in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic in Hong Kong pushed the Hang Seng Index to a nearly two-year low at the end of February. Meanwhile, the CNH debt market in Hong Kong continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market softened from mid-2021, partly affected by weaker asset market sentiment and a new wave of the local pandemic. Major global equity markets generally continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, taking the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). The global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings amid monetary and fiscal policy stimulus supported the rally in major global equity markets, although the pandemic remained a key risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, major global equity markets consolidated from early January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies in the face of surging inflation risks, sharp increases in commodity prices, and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. In contrast, the Hong Kong equity market continued to lag behind other major global equity markets towards the end of 2021. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November and closed at 23,398 at the end of 2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, renewed buying interest from value investors in the Hong Kong equity market drove the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding the development of the pandemic in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index to a nearly two-year low of 22,713 points at the end of February. Over the entire review period from the end of August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index declined by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index fell by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index Equity market option-implied volatility fluctuated sharply in late November 2021 due to the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, before easing subsequently. Although the SKEW Index retreated from its record high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investors’ concerns over a correction in the prolonged equity market rally since the outbreak of the pandemic and their willingness to pay more to hedge against downside risks in the equity market (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatilities of the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500 Index, and the SKEW Index Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, the Hong Kong equity market continued to record net inflows from international investors since the previous report (Chart 4.13). In contrast, Southbound Stock Connect recorded substantial net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns over the impact of changes in Mainland regulation on technology stocks. However, buying flows through Southbound Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, with total inflows reaching HK$98.3 billion by the end of February. During the review period, the cumulative net buying amount increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net equity market fund inflows into Hong Kong Chart 4.14 Net flows through Stock Connect Hong Kong’s primary market slowed in the second half of 2021 after raising a record amount of funds in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, there were 98 initial public offerings, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), with the total amount of funds raised declining by 17.8% from the preceding year. In 2021, the Hong Kong Stock Exchange ranked fourth in the global IPO market, behind only Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Initial public offering market in Hong Kong The outlook for the local equity market remains uncertain. The easing of Mainland monetary policy and more secondary listings in Hong Kong by US-listed Chinese companies in the primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong equity market. However, the equity market continues to face numerous headwinds, including uncertainties surrounding the development of the local pandemic, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio increased slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by historical and international standards. Underpinned by sound capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, the HKMA extended various support measures to further assist the economy through the difficult period. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, while the risk of a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation will also pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impacts of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% in the second half of 2021 compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profitability was mainly attributable to lower net interest and non-interest income and higher operating expenses. Accordingly, the return on assets declined to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while the return on assets declined to 0.59% from 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Reflecting the persistent low-interest-rate environment, the net interest margin of retail banks also remained low at 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA’s additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills, HIBORs increased slightly in the final quarter of 2021. However, as liquidity in the banking system remained highly abundant, HIBORs continued to stay at low levels. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR increased slightly by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at the end of December 2021 (see the blue line in Chart 5.3). Retail banks’ funding costs remained stable during the review period. In particular, the composite interest rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks) increased modestly by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at the end of 2021 (the green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. (c) Since June 2019, the composite interest rate has been calculated based on the new local “interest rate risk in the banking book” (IRRBB) framework. As such, figures from June 2019 onwards are not strictly comparable with those of previous months. From a broader perspective, the overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost for licensed banks in Hong Kong increased slightly by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost has been calculated as the weighted average of the relevant figures for these two groups of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. While US monetary policy normalisation may signal an improvement in bank profitability, the near-term improvement may be partly offset by two factors. First, although the US Fed indicated that it would raise interest rates multiple times in 2022, past experience suggests that movements in local interest rates may lag behind those in US interest rates, particularly when interbank liquidity in Hong Kong remains highly abundant. It may therefore take more time for banks’ net interest margins to improve. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may create uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery, thereby exerting pressure on banks’ asset quality and profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector continued to be strong and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.2% at the end of 2021 (Chart 5.5), well above the international minimum requirement of 8%. The Tier 1 capital ratio and the Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio were 18.2% and 16.2% respectively during the period. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs recorded a healthy level of 7.9% at the end of 2021, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3%. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. With effect from 1 January 2013, locally incorporated AIs are required to comply with the revised Basel III capital adequacy framework. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. The liquidity positions of the banking sector, as measured by the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 151.9% in the fourth quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.6), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 59.1% during the same period, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The latest Net Stable Funding Ratios also reflected the stable funding positions of AIs. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.3% in the third quarter of 2021 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of category 2A institutions also recorded a high level of 150.4%, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75%. The data suggest that the Hong Kong banking sector is well positioned to withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.7 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for AIs. At the end of 2021, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all AIs hovered at 57.6%, close to the level of 57.2% six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 The liability structure of all AIs 1. Figures may not add up to the total due to rounding. 2. Figures refer to percentages of total liabilities, including capital and reserves. 3. Debt securities comprise negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. In the second half of 2021, total deposits in the banking sector were broadly unchanged, while total loans and advances decreased slightly. As a result, the average all-currency loan-to-deposit ratio of the banking sector declined modestly to 71.8% at the end of 2021 from 74.1% at the end of June 2021 (Chart 5.9). The decline in the loan-to-deposit ratio was mainly attributable to a decrease in the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio during the same period, which more than offset the increase in the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio. Reflecting a decrease in foreign currency loans and a corresponding increase in deposits, the average foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 57.5% at the end of 2021 from 63.3% six months earlier. By contrast, as the decline in Hong Kong dollar deposits exceeded that in Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio increased slightly to 86.7% from 84.2% six months earlier.
